skills.presentation: Low back pain with unilateral (or bilateral) lower limb radiating pain along the course of the sciatic nerve (from the buttock and posterior thigh, along the lateral lower leg, radiating to the dorsum or sole of the foot); pain worsens with cough, sneeze, straining to defecate, and other Valsalva maneuvers that increase intra-abdominal pressure; worse with standing and walking, relieved by bed rest; accompanied by numbness, decreased sensation, and muscle weakness in the innervated area of the affected lower limb nerves; in severe cases, cauda equina syndrome occurs (perineal numbness, decreased saddle-area sensation, bowel and bladder dysfunction, and sexual dysfunction).

first_questions: Does the low back pain radiate with numbness or pain down the buttock and posterior thigh to the lower leg or sole of the foot?
When you cough, sneeze, or strain to pass stool, does the low back and leg pain suddenly worsen with a pulling or shooting sensation?
Is the low back and leg pain noticeably relieved when you rest lying on a firm mattress? Does it worsen after standing for a long time or walking a lot?
followup_questions: Do your toes (big toe bending upward or pressing downward) have strength? Is there numbness or reduced sensation on the dorsum or sole of the foot?

Are you unable to pass stool or urine, or do you have urinary incontinence? Is there numbness in the buttock and perineal area (the area that contacts a bicycle saddle)? (Extremely urgent: rule out cauda equina syndrome)
Do you have a history of heavy lifting, prolonged sitting with bending forward, or lumbar sprain/trauma?
stop_conditions: Radicular radiating pain has been clearly localized to a nerve distribution level (L4/5 or L5/S1), and mechanical compression triggers have been identified
Acute cauda equina compression emergency has been rigorously ruled out
Previous response to conservative treatment and the degree of neurologic deficit have been fully documented

essential: Orthopedic specialty physical examination (positive straight-leg raise test and augmentation test (Lasègue sign), femoral nerve stretch test, deep tenderness beside the spinous process at the affected level with radiation to the lower limb, tendon reflex and motor/sensory examination)
High-resolution lumbar magnetic resonance imaging (noncontrast MRI, clear visualization of disc bulge/protrusion/extrusion, dural sac and nerve root compression and edema; gold standard)
Anteroposterior and lateral lumbar spine plain radiographs (to assess lumbar physiological curvature, disc space height, degeneration, and to exclude fracture and bone destruction)
if_suspected: Noncontrast lumbar CT plus 3D reconstruction (clear evaluation of disc calcification, ligamentum flavum ossification, and osteophyte/facet joint bony changes)
Electromyography and nerve conduction velocity (EMG) of both lower limbs (to differentiate peripheral nerve entrapment disorders such as piriformis syndrome and diabetic peripheral neuropathy)
avoid: Blindly ordering whole-body large-field bone scans in patients with isolated low back and leg pain
Blindly and roughly applying high-force rotational manipulation/reduction massage during an acute severe attack (highly likely to cause disc extrusion/rupture and acute paralysis)

first_line: For first episode or mild-to-moderate disease, conservative treatment is preferred: strict bed rest on a firm mattress during the acute phase and external protection with a lumbar corset

Anti-inflammatory analgesia (oral celecoxib/diclofenac sodium) + resolution of nerve edema (short-term dexamethasone or mannitol as a dehydrating agent) + neurotrophic therapy (mecobalamin tablets) + physical traction therapy

Surgery for patients with no response after 3 months of conservative treatment, frequent recurrence, or progressive worsening of neurologic injury (preferred: minimally invasive spinal endoscopic discectomy PELD/UBE, or open spinal canal decompression with fusion and internal fixation).
safety_warnings: Once cauda equina syndrome occurs (bowel and bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, flaccid paralysis of the lower limbs), it is an orthopedic emergency; emergency surgical decompression must be performed within 24-48 hours; delay can cause lifelong bowel and bladder incontinence and paralysis
Absolutely prohibit rough high-force massage and rotational manipulation/reduction during the acute edema phase

Long-term use of a lumbar corset should not exceed 3-4 weeks, to avoid disuse atrophy of the core lumbar back muscles; during remission, strengthen lumbar back muscle exercises such as the 'little swallow' prone extension and five-point support
personalization: Young patients with simple single-level soft disc herniation: preferentially choose minimally invasive percutaneous transforaminal/interlaminar endoscopic discectomy
Patients with obvious lumbar spondylolysis or unstable lumbar spondylolisthesis: require spinal canal decompression + interbody bone graft fusion and internal fixation (TLIF)
Elderly patients with severe osteoporosis: avoid vigorous traction and focus on systemic osteoporosis treatment

skills.presentation: Neck and shoulder pain and aching discomfort, radiating to the upper limb, forearm, and fingers, as stabbing or electric shock-like radiating pain or numbness; limited neck movement, with exacerbation of upper limb radiating pain when the head and neck rotate toward the affected side or extend backward; numbness and weakness of the fingers on the affected side and clumsiness in holding objects; physical examination shows tenderness beside the cervical spine with radiation to the affected limb, positive cervical compression test (Spurling sign), positive brachial plexus stretch test (Eaton sign), and diminished tendon reflexes.

first_questions: Does the neck and shoulder pain radiate with numbness or pain down the arm and forearm to the fingers? Which specific fingers are numb?
When you extend your neck backward or turn your head toward the painful side, does the numbness and pain in your arm suddenly worsen like an electric shock?
Are you still nimble when holding chopsticks, buttoning clothes, or writing? Is there wasting or weakness of the hand muscles?
followup_questions: When walking, do you feel as if you are stepping on cotton, with unsteady gait and easy falls? Do you feel as if your chest and abdomen are bound and tightened by a rope? (Extremely critical: rule out cervical spondylotic myelopathy)
Does your work usually require prolonged head-down posture looking at a computer, using a mobile phone, or leaning over a desk?
Is your pillow high when you sleep at night? Is the pain relieved or worsened when you raise your arm above your head?
stop_conditions: The affected level of nerve root radiating pain (C5/C6/C7/C8) and mechanical compression-provoked signs have been clearly identified
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy (cotton-stepping sensation, pyramidal tract signs) and peripheral nerve entrapment have been rigorously excluded
The trigger of prolonged desk work posture and previous history of physical traction treatment have been clearly obtained

essential: Orthopedic specialty physical examination (cervical compression test Spurling sign, brachial plexus stretch test Eaton sign, Hoffmann sign to differentiate myelopathy)
High-resolution cervical MRI (to identify the site of disc herniation, uncovertebral joint osteophytes, and corresponding nerve root compression and edema)
Anteroposterior and lateral plus bilateral oblique cervical spine radiographs (to assess cervical physiological curvature, degree of intervertebral foramen stenosis, and bone hyperplasia)
if_suspected: Noncontrast cervical CT plus 3D reconstruction (to assess ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament [OPLL] and the morphology of posterior vertebral body osteophytes)
Upper limb electromyography and nerve conduction velocity (EMG) (to differentiate carpal tunnel syndrome, cubital tunnel syndrome, and thoracic outlet syndrome)
avoid: Blindly performing large-amplitude forceful rotational manipulation/massage in patients with cervical spondylosis without physical examination and MRI (highly likely to cause high-level paraplegia and death)
Blindly ordering whole-brain cerebral angiography for isolated neck and shoulder pain

first_line: For the vast majority of patients, comprehensive nonoperative conservative treatment is preferred: correction of poor head-down posture and intermittent cervical traction with a halter
Cervical collar immobilization
Anti-inflammatory analgesia (selective COX-2 inhibitor celecoxib)
Resolution of nerve root edema (aescin [horse chestnut seed extract] or short-term low-dose oral corticosteroids)
Neurotrophic therapy (mecobalamin tablets)
Muscle relaxant (eperisone)

Surgery for patients in whom conservative treatment is ineffective and severe pain affects work and daily life, or who have severe muscle atrophy (anterior cervical discectomy and fusion [ACDF] or posterior cervical foraminotomy and decompression).
safety_warnings: Absolutely prohibit blind, rough high-force cervical rotational manipulation in patients with cervical spondylosis; otherwise, acute spinal cord injury and lifelong paraplegia are highly likely

If the patient has a cotton-stepping sensation, unsteady gait, and a positive Hoffmann sign suggesting cervical spondylotic myelopathy, traction and massage are strictly prohibited, and surgical decompression should be performed as early as possible
Cervical traction must be performed under the guidance of a specialist physician, with appropriate angle and weight adjustment; if dizziness or worsening hand numbness occurs, stop immediately
personalization: Young and middle-aged patients with single-level herniation: evaluate for artificial cervical disc replacement (ACDR) to preserve cervical segment mobility
Elderly patients with multilevel degeneration and severe osteophyte hyperplasia: anterior decompression and fusion (ACDF) is preferred
Sedentary office workers: instruct them to perform neck extension stretching exercises every 45 minutes of work and adjust computer screen height

skills.presentation: Commonly affects weight-bearing, frequently used joints such as the knee, hip, distal interphalangeal joints, and lumbar spine; mainly manifests as chronic dull pain in the affected joints, initially 'rest pain' or 'start-up pain' (pain is obvious when getting up in the morning or just standing up after prolonged sitting, improves after a little activity, but worsens again after excessive activity); joint stiffness (morning stiffness is short in duration, generally <30 minutes); joint swelling, tenderness, crepitus/crepitation on movement, and restricted joint range of motion; in advanced stages, bony joint deformities such as genu varum ('O-shaped legs') occur.

first_questions: How long have you had a dull ache in your knee or hip joint? Is the pain especially severe when going up or down stairs or when squatting down and standing up?
When you first get out of bed in the morning or stand up after sitting for a long time, do your joints feel stiff and hard? Do they feel a little better after moving for a few minutes?
How long does the morning joint stiffness usually last? (Does it resolve within half an hour? This helps differentiate rheumatoid arthritis)
followup_questions: When you move your knee, do you hear or feel a crunching sound of bone rubbing against bone (crepitus)?
Does your knee often feel sore and swollen, or even feel hot and fluid-filled to the touch? Has your knee become deformed and bowed into an O shape?
Is your usual level of physical activity high? Do you often climb mountains or stairs, lift heavy objects, or have a history of prolonged exposure to cold?
stop_conditions: The affected weight-bearing joints, the pattern of load-related/start-up pain, and the characteristic morning stiffness <30 minutes have been clearly identified
The degree of joint deformity and level of functional impairment have been assessed
Rheumatoid arthritis, septic arthritis, and gouty arthritis have been excluded

essential: Weight-bearing (standing) plain radiographs of the affected joints (core examination: asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and cystic changes, and marginal osteophyte formation/bone spurs)
Orthopedic specialty physical examination (joint line tenderness, patellar ballottement test to assess effusion, range of motion [ROM], and crepitus)
if_suspected: High-resolution joint MRI (for early assessment of articular cartilage degeneration and wear thickness, meniscal injury/tears, and synovitis-related effusion)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and rheumatoid factor (RF) (to differentiate inflammatory joint disease)
Joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis (to rule out gout and septic infection when there is marked joint swelling and effusion)
avoid: Obtaining only supine radiographs without standing weight-bearing X-rays, leading to underestimation of joint space narrowing
Ordering high-dose whole-body ECT radionuclide scanning for isolated osteoarthritis without suspected metastasis

first_line: Stepwise comprehensive treatment: foundational treatment (weight reduction to reduce joint load, avoidance of frequent mountain climbing, stair climbing, and deep squatting, use of a cane/crutch/knee brace, and quadriceps isometric strengthening exercises)
Pharmacologic treatment: topical NSAID gels/patches (flurbiprofen gel patch, diclofenac diethylamine emulsion) are preferred
Oral NSAIDs (celecoxib, diclofenac sodium)
Cartilage-protective agent (glucosamine sulfate)
Intra-articular injection (sodium hyaluronate to lubricate the joint, or short-term glucocorticoid injection during acute inflammation)
Surgery for advanced severe joint deformity with loss of function (artificial hip/knee joint arthroplasty TKA/THA or high tibial osteotomy HTO).
safety_warnings: Oral NSAIDs should be used at the lowest effective dose; elderly patients and those with a history of ulcers must receive concomitant PPI therapy to protect the gastric mucosa

The number of intra-articular glucocorticoid injections per year must be strictly controlled to no more than 2-3 times; overly frequent injections can accelerate articular cartilage destruction and cause joint infection
Intra-articular injection must be performed under strict aseptic conditions to prevent iatrogenic septic arthritis
personalization: Young and middle-aged patients with mild-to-moderate medial unicompartmental knee osteoarthritis and varus deformity: knee-preserving surgery may be performed (high tibial osteotomy HTO or unicompartmental knee arthroplasty UKA)
Elderly patients with advanced severe tricompartmental osteoarthritis and severe O-shaped leg deformity: total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is preferred
Patients with early mild disease: mainly straight-leg raise quadriceps strengthening exercises + weight reduction + topical anti-inflammatory patches

skills.presentation: The patient reports pain at the posterior heel or lower segment of the lower leg, often worsened with the first step in the morning or after exercise. Typical findings are localized tenderness and swelling; in some patients, tendon thickening or a friction sensation (crepitus) may be palpable. Pain is relieved at rest and worsens with strenuous exercise; severe cases may have difficulty walking or limping.

first_questions: Where exactly is the pain located in the heel? Did it start suddenly or gradually worsen?
Have you recently increased your exercise volume, changed footwear, or undergone high-intensity training?
followup_questions: Do you feel marked stiffness or pain with your first step out of bed in the morning?
Is there sharp pain when pressing the affected area, or do you hear a friction sound?
stop_conditions: The pain location, triggers, and relationship to activity have been clearly identified, and there is no history of acute rupture.
The patient has described typical morning stiffness and worsening after exercise, and no further questioning is needed.
Emergencies such as Achilles tendon rupture (e.g., hearing a pop and being unable to stand on tiptoe) have been excluded.

essential: Physical examination: palpation of the Achilles tendon tender point, observation of local swelling, assessment of ankle range of motion, and heel-raise test.
Ultrasonography: assess Achilles tendon thickness, echogenicity changes, and presence of tear.
if_suspected: MRI: for complex cases or suspected partial/complete rupture, clearly showing the extent of soft tissue injury.
Plain radiographs: to exclude retrocalcaneal bursitis, Haglund deformity, or bone spurs and other bony lesions.
avoid: Routine CT scanning: low soft tissue resolution, not first-line, and associated with higher radiation exposure.
Blind aspiration: unless septic bursitis is highly suspected, it can easily cause iatrogenic injury.

first_line: First-line treatment is mainly conservative and includes the RICE principle in the acute phase (rest, ice, compression, elevation), combined with NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 1-2 weeks) to control inflammation. The core intervention is eccentric Achilles tendon training (e.g., drop-down exercises on a step), 2 sets daily, 15 repetitions per set, for at least 12 weeks. Avoid returning to vigorous running and jumping too early; use a heel pad or orthopedic insole if necessary to reduce traction.
safety_warnings: Do not apply heat or forceful massage during the acute phase of redness, swelling, heat, and pain, to avoid aggravating inflammation.
Long-term use of NSAIDs requires attention to the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding; use with caution in patients with a history of ulcers.
Do not inject glucocorticoids into the Achilles tendon; this may increase tendon fragility and even cause rupture.
personalization: Elderly patients need assessment of osteoporosis and fall risk, and training intensity should be progressed gradually.
Patients with diabetes need strict blood glucose monitoring because hyperglycemia may delay soft tissue healing.
Athletes need rehabilitation plans adjusted to the characteristics of their sport, with gradual transition to sport-specific training.

skills.presentation: Patients often report sudden severe pain posterior to the heel during exercise, as if kicked or struck, followed by inability to tiptoe, weakness with push-off, or difficulty walking. On examination, local swelling and bruising posterior to the heel are visible, a depression indicating discontinuity of the tendon can be palpated, and the patient cannot perform a single-leg heel raise.

first_questions: Did you hear a 'pop' at the time of injury?
Can you now stand on the toes of the affected side or raise your heel?
followup_questions: Where exactly is the pain located posterior to the heel?
Were you performing explosive movements (such as basketball jumping or sprinting) before the injury?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes hearing a rupture sound and is unable to perform a single-leg heel raise
The injury mechanism has been confirmed as acute violent trauma and the symptoms are typical
Physical examination reveals an obvious Achilles tendon depression and a positive Thompson test

essential: Physical examination: Thompson test (squeeze the calf muscles and observe the foot response)
Physical examination: palpation (palpate Achilles tendon continuity)
Ultrasound examination (high-frequency ultrasound to assess the degree of tendon rupture and the distance between the torn ends)
if_suspected: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging, for complex cases or differential diagnosis of chronic rupture)
Plain radiography (to exclude concomitant fracture or bony abnormalities)
avoid: Routine CT scanning (low resolution for soft tissues, not first-line)
Blind Achilles tendon needle biopsy (increases infection risk and is unnecessary)

first_line: Choose surgical repair or conservative treatment according to the type of rupture. Surgery is indicated for young active patients, with Achilles tendon suture

Conservative treatment is suitable for elderly or less active patients, using a long leg cast immobilized in plantar flexion for 6 weeks, followed by gradual functional exercise. Postoperatively, physical therapy is needed to restore joint range of motion and muscle strength; the course usually lasts 3-6 months.
safety_warnings: Avoid early weight-bearing, which can cause re-rupture
Be alert for deep vein thrombosis, especially during prolonged immobilization
Pay attention to the risk of wound infection, especially with improper postoperative care
personalization: Patients with diabetes need strict blood glucose control to promote wound healing
If elderly patients have comorbid osteoporosis, adjust the intensity of rehabilitation training to prevent fracture
Athletes need a prolonged rehabilitation period to ensure explosive power when returning to competition

skills.presentation: Patients often present with obvious short-limb dwarfism, especially shortening of the proximal limbs (thighs and upper arms), while trunk length is relatively normal. Typical signs include frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge with a saddle nose, and fingers separated in a 'trident' pattern. Affected children usually have short stature, obvious genu varum or valgum when standing, and increased lumbar lordosis. Some patients may report lower limb numbness or intermittent claudication due to spinal stenosis.

first_questions: Has the child's height growth curve been persistently below the 3rd percentile for peers?
Is there a family history of similar short stature or skeletal deformity?
Does the child currently have difficulty walking, lower limb pain, or abnormal gait?
followup_questions: If lower limb numbness or weakness occurs, ask whether the symptoms are related to the duration of standing or walking?
If there is breathing difficulty or severe snoring during sleep, ask whether there is awakening with breath-holding at night or difficulty swallowing?
If intellectual development is delayed, ask about the specific manifestations and whether language impairment is present?
stop_conditions: Typical physical features (such as short limbs, macrocephaly, and trident hands) have been identified and imaging has confirmed long bone changes.
FGFR3 genetic testing has been completed and a pathogenic mutation has been confirmed.
Major complications (such as spinal cord compression and apnea) have been assessed and an initial management plan has been formulated.

essential: Skeletal survey plain radiography (focusing on the morphology of long bones, pelvis, and spine)
FGFR3 gene sequencing (gold standard for diagnosis)
Cranial MRI or CT (to assess basilar invagination and hydrocephalus)
if_suspected: Whole-spine MRI (to assess spinal stenosis and the degree of spinal cord compression)
Polysomnography (PSG, to screen for obstructive sleep apnea)
Audiological testing (to assess conductive or sensorineural hearing loss)
avoid: Whole-body bone density scanning without indication (this is not an osteoporotic disease)
Routine invasive joint aspiration (unless concomitant infection is suspected)
Overreliance on serum calcium and phosphorus metabolism indicators (results are usually normal)

first_line: There is currently no curative medication; first-line treatment is mainly multidisciplinary comprehensive management. For growth restriction, recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy may be considered, usually at a dose of 0.05 mg/kg/day by subcutaneous injection, continued for several years with monitoring of IGF-1 levels. For severe spinal stenosis or hydrocephalus, timely decompression surgery or shunt placement is required. Non-pharmacological interventions include physical therapy to improve muscle strength and balance, and avoidance of strenuous weight-bearing exercise to prevent fracture.
safety_warnings: When using growth hormone, be alert for the risk of worsening intracranial hypertension; funduscopic examination and head circumference should be monitored regularly before and during treatment.
Extreme caution is required during anesthesia induction because abnormal airway anatomy can easily lead to difficult intubation; an experienced anesthesiologist is recommended.
Avoid any elective surgery or high-intensity rehabilitation training during acute respiratory infection.
personalization: In infancy, focus on airway management and feeding guidance to prevent choking risk.
School-age children need adjustment of brace-wearing plans and activity restrictions according to the progression of scoliosis.
Adult patients require lifelong monitoring for symptoms of lumbar spinal stenosis, with early intervention when necessary to avoid permanent neurological damage.

skills.presentation: Patients report severe pain above the shoulder, especially aggravated when raising the arm or lifting heavy objects. An obvious prominence or step-like deformity at the acromion may be visible, with local swelling and tenderness. The affected arm is often adducted close to the trunk because of pain, active abduction is limited, and passive movement can provoke severe pain. Some patients have a palpable upward tilt of the distal clavicle.

first_questions: At the time of injury, was there a direct impact to the shoulder or a fall onto an outstretched hand?
Is there currently an obvious 'step-like' deformity or swelling of the shoulder?
Can you raise your arm actively, or are you completely unable to move it because of pain?
followup_questions: If you have numbness, please describe its exact location and duration.
After the injury, have you attempted self-reduction or heat application?
Do you have a history of fracture or dislocation of the same shoulder?
stop_conditions: The trauma mechanism has been clarified and physical examination reveals typical acromial prominence deformity.
Imaging examination (X-ray) has confirmed the degree of joint separation and classification.
The patient has no symptoms of neurovascular injury and vital signs are stable.

essential: Anteroposterior shoulder X-ray
Zanca view X-ray
Bilateral comparative shoulder X-rays
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the shoulder (to assess subtle fractures and ligament injury)
MRI examination (to assess the integrity of the coracoclavicular ligaments and rotator cuff)
Ultrasound examination (dynamic observation of soft tissue injury)
avoid: Blind manual reduction
Strong traction before fracture has been excluded
Routine use of anticoagulants to prevent thrombosis (unless there is a clear indication)

first_line: Grade I-II injuries are treated conservatively: immobilization with a sling for 2-3 weeks, combined with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as ibuprofen 0.4 g tid) to relieve pain, with early pendulum exercises to prevent stiffness. Grade III and above or grade V-VI injuries usually require surgery, with coracoclavicular ligament reconstruction or distal clavicle excision and fixation. Strict rehabilitation training is required after surgery, and early weight-bearing should be avoided.
safety_warnings: Do not forcefully reduce severe acute dislocation, to prevent brachial plexus injury.
When using NSAIDs, be alert for the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, especially in elderly patients.
If finger numbness, coldness, or pallor occurs after surgery, immediately evaluate for vascular or nerve compression.
personalization: For athletes or heavy manual laborers, consider a lower surgical threshold, prioritizing functional recovery.
In elderly patients with osteoporosis, use internal fixation screws with caution; consider hook plate or autologous tendon grafting.
Patients with comorbid diabetes need strict blood glucose control to promote wound healing.

skills.presentation: Patients report persistent dull shoulder pain that worsens at night and affects sleep. A typical feature is marked limitation of both active and passive range of motion, especially difficulty with external rotation, abduction, and extension, presenting a 'frozen' state. The disease course is often divided into a painful phase, a stiff phase, and a resolution phase; there is usually no obvious history of trauma, and it is more common in people aged 40-60 years, with a high incidence in patients with diabetes.

first_questions: How long has your shoulder pain lasted? Do you wake up at night because of the pain?
Can you comb your hair or reach your back by yourself? Do you feel catching when raising your arm or rotating it outward?
followup_questions: Do you have a recent history of diabetes, thyroid disease, or shoulder trauma?
Did the pain worsen gradually or occur suddenly? Have you had previous episodes of frozen shoulder?
stop_conditions: The nature of the pain, degree of motion limitation, and duration have been clarified, and obvious trauma has been excluded.
It has been confirmed that there are no signs of acute infection (such as high fever, redness, swelling, heat, and pain).
Underlying diseases (such as diabetes) have been understood sufficiently to formulate an initial diagnosis and treatment plan.

essential: Shoulder X-ray (anteroposterior and axillary views)
Physical examination: assess active and passive range of motion (ROM)
Neer sign and Hawkins-Kennedy test
if_suspected: Shoulder MRI (to exclude rotator cuff tear and labral injury)
Ultrasound examination (to assess synovial thickening and joint capsule effusion)
Blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin testing (to screen for diabetes)
avoid: Routine CT scanning (low resolution for soft tissues, not first-line)
Unnecessary intra-articular contrast arthrography (unless hydrodilatation is planned)
Complex imaging studies before blind forceful manual release

first_line: First-line treatment is mainly conservative, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as celecoxib 200 mg qd for 2-4 weeks) to relieve pain. The core intervention is physical therapy, with daily pendulum exercises, wall-climbing exercises, and joint capsule stretching, avoiding forceful traction. If pain is severe, intra-articular glucocorticoid injection of the shoulder (such as triamcinolone acetonide 10-20 mg) may be considered, combined with oral medication; rehabilitation training usually needs to be maintained for 3-6 months.
safety_warnings: Hormone injection requires strict aseptic technique; avoid repeated injections that can lead to tendon rupture or blood glucose fluctuation.
NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with peptic ulcer or severe renal insufficiency.
During rehabilitation training, do not use force to forcibly break through the pain limit, to prevent fracture or soft tissue tear.
personalization: Patients with diabetes need strict blood glucose control; otherwise, treatment efficacy is poor and recurrence is likely.
In elderly patients with osteoporosis, use hormone injection with caution and prioritize gentle physical therapy.
For those with high occupational demands (such as athletes), early intervention with manipulation under anesthesia may be considered.

skills.disease: adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder (frozen shoulder)

skills.presentation: Patients often report sudden inversion or eversion of the foot while walking or exercising, followed by severe pain, swelling, and limited range of motion. Typical findings include marked localized tenderness, especially at the anteroinferior aspect of the lateral malleolus (anterior talofibular ligament) or below the medial malleolus (deltoid ligament); some patients may hear a tearing sound, with subcutaneous ecchymosis and difficulty bearing weight.

first_questions: What was the exact movement at the time of injury? Did you hear a sound?
Can you stand or walk independently now? Where is the pain most severe?
followup_questions: Have you had a similar injury before?
Did obvious swelling or bruising develop immediately after the injury?
stop_conditions: Clear trauma mechanism and no neurovascular symptoms
Confirmed inability to bear weight with obvious deformity
Mild symptoms that do not affect daily activities

essential: Ankle radiographs (to exclude fracture)
Physical examination: palpation of tender points and assessment of joint stability
if_suspected: Ankle MRI (if complete ligament rupture or cartilage injury is suspected)
Ultrasound (to assess soft tissue swelling and effusion)
avoid: Routine CT scanning (unless occult fracture is highly suspected)
Unnecessary MRI (not first-line for mild sprain)

first_line: In the acute phase, follow the RICE principle (rest, ice, compression, elevation). Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen 0.2g orally three times daily to relieve pain, for no more than 7 days. Use a brace for 2-3 weeks and avoid early weight bearing. Later, rehabilitation training to restore range of motion and muscle strength.
safety_warnings: Contraindicated in patients allergic to NSAIDs
Long-term high-dose use may cause gastrointestinal bleeding
Patients with diabetes should be alert to infection risk
personalization: Use anticoagulants with caution in older adults to prevent exacerbation of bleeding
Children require dose adjustment and close monitoring of growth
Athletes require a prolonged rehabilitation period to prevent recurrence

skills.presentation: Patients often report joint pain, swelling, stiffness, and limited range of motion. Joint stiffness is prominent on waking and lasts more than 30 minutes, with slight relief after activity. Some patients have local warmth or redness and swelling; in severe cases, daily walking or fine hand movements are affected.

first_questions: Where exactly is your joint pain?
Is the pain accompanied by swelling or redness?
How long does joint stiffness last when you get up in the morning?
followup_questions: Does the pain worsen at night?
Is there a family history of similar symptoms?
Have you had any recent trauma or infection?
stop_conditions: Symptoms are clearly described and there are no manifestations of other systemic diseases
The location and duration of pain have been clarified
The patient has no further information to add

essential: X-ray examination
Blood inflammatory marker tests (such as CRP, ESR)
Synovial fluid analysis
if_suspected: MRI examination
Rheumatoid factor testing
HLA-B27 gene testing
avoid: Routine CT scanning (unless fracture is suspected)
Unnecessary whole-body PET-CT
Repeated joint aspiration

first_line: First-line treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 2-4 weeks
Combine with physical therapy (hot compresses, cold compresses) and moderate exercise. In severe cases, short-term glucocorticoid injection may be used.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of high-dose NSAIDs to prevent gastrointestinal bleeding
Be aware of interactions between drugs and anticoagulants
Monitor for abnormal liver and kidney function
personalization: Older patients should reduce the NSAID dose and receive enhanced gastric protection
NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnant women; use acetaminophen instead
Use NSAIDs with caution in patients with renal insufficiency

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe heel pain and inability to bear weight or walk. On examination, marked heel swelling and ecchymosis are visible, with significant localized tenderness; squeezing both sides of the heel can provoke severe pain (positive lateral compression sign). If it is an intra-articular fracture, flattening or widening deformity of the sole may be present. Some patients have concomitant spinal fractures due to high-energy trauma, so manifestations of polytrauma should be considered.

first_questions: How did the injury happen? Is there a history of falling from a height?
Can you stand or walk after the injury? How severe is the pain?
Is there obvious swelling or deformity of the foot?
followup_questions: Do you have numbness in the sole of the foot or difficulty moving your toes?
Was the injury accompanied by low back pain or loss of consciousness?
Do you have a history of diabetes or osteoporosis?
stop_conditions: A fall-from-height mechanism and typical heel swelling and pain symptoms have been clearly elicited
No signs of neurovascular injury or risk of concomitant spinal injury have been confirmed
The patient's complaints are highly consistent with physical examination signs and there are no other systemic abnormalities

essential: Axial calcaneus radiograph
Lateral calcaneus radiograph
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the calcaneus
if_suspected: Whole-spine X-ray or CT (to screen for thoracolumbar compression fractures)
Lower extremity vascular ultrasound (to assess blood supply)
Ankle MRI (when ligament injury is suspected)
avoid: Early weight-bearing functional testing of the foot
Blind manual reduction procedures
Unnecessary open soft tissue exploration

first_line: In the acute phase, strictly immobilize, elevate the affected limb, and apply ice to reduce swelling. Nondisplaced fractures are treated with cast immobilization for 6-8 weeks

Patients with obvious displacement or articular surface collapse require open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF). After surgery, anticoagulation therapy is used to prevent thrombosis, and NSAIDs are given for analgesia according to pain severity. Rehabilitation training should progress gradually under a doctor's guidance, avoiding early weight bearing that may lead to internal fixation failure.
safety_warnings: Do not force surgery before swelling subsides, to prevent skin necrosis
Patients with diabetes require strict blood glucose control to reduce infection risk
Patients on prolonged bed rest must receive deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis
personalization: For older patients with osteoporosis, consider augmented screws or bone cement augmentation
Smokers should stop smoking before surgery to reduce the risk of poor wound healing
Patients with bilateral fractures should be assessed early for pelvic stability and walking aids

skills.presentation: Patients often report numbness and tingling in the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and radial side of the ring finger, worsening at night, with prominent symptoms on waking that are relieved by shaking the hand. Some patients have hand weakness and reduced grip strength; in severe cases, thenar muscle atrophy occurs. Typical findings are sensory abnormalities in the median nerve distribution, and symptoms are related to wrist activity or posture.

first_questions: Do your fingers have numbness or tingling? Which fingers specifically?
Do the symptoms worsen at night or in the early morning? Are they relieved by shaking your hand?
followup_questions: Do you have hand weakness or frequently drop things?
Are the symptoms related to prolonged use of a computer or mobile phone or repetitive hand movements?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes numbness in the typical median nerve distribution that worsens at night.
Symptoms have been confirmed to be related to specific hand activities or postures.
The patient has no history of other neurological diseases or systemic diseases (such as diabetes) that could interfere with diagnosis.

essential: Phalen test
Tinel sign examination
Nerve conduction velocity testing
if_suspected: Ultrasound (to assess median nerve compression)
MRI (to exclude other space-occupying lesions)
Electromyography (to further assess the degree of nerve injury)
avoid: X-ray examination (unless fracture or bony structural abnormality is suspected)
Routine blood tests (unless systemic disease is suspected)
Unnecessary imaging scans (such as CT without clear indications)

first_line: First-line treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 2-4 weeks) and local corticosteroid injection (such as triamcinolone acetonide 10 mg). At the same time, wearing a wrist brace for immobilization is recommended, and repetitive hand movements should be avoided. If conservative treatment is ineffective, consider surgical decompression.
safety_warnings: Long-term use of NSAIDs requires vigilance for the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
Corticosteroid injection may cause local infection or skin atrophy.
Patients with diabetes need to monitor blood glucose changes.
personalization: Pregnant women may preferentially choose physical therapy and brace immobilization, avoiding drug intervention.
Older adults should be aware of osteoporosis risk and use glucocorticoid drugs with caution.
Workers whose jobs involve hand use should adjust their working posture and take more rest.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of pain, numbness, or weakness in the neck, shoulder, and upper limb; symptoms may radiate to the fingers. Pain is usually persistent dull or sharp and is aggravated by neck movement; some patients have muscle atrophy or decreased grip strength. Typical features include awakening at night with pain and difficulty raising the arm.

first_questions: When did your pain start?
Does the pain radiate to your arm or fingers?
followup_questions: Do you have numbness or weakness in your hand?
Which movements worsen or relieve the pain?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described the location, nature, and triggers of the pain.
The duration of symptoms and associated symptoms (such as numbness or weakness) have been ascertained.
The patient has provided clear answers about past medical history and medication use.

essential: Cervical spine X-ray
Cervical spine MRI
Electromyography
if_suspected: Cervical spine CT scan
Nerve conduction velocity study
avoid: Unnecessary radionuclide scanning
Nonspecific blood tests

first_line: First-line treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 2 weeks) to reduce inflammation and pain, combined with physical therapy (such as hot compresses and traction) to improve local blood circulation. If necessary, a muscle relaxant (such as eperisone 50 mg three times daily) may be used short-term.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of NSAIDs to prevent gastrointestinal bleeding.
Pay attention to drug interactions, especially in patients using anticoagulants.
Monitor for serious adverse reactions, such as abnormal liver and kidney function.
personalization: Older adults require reduced drug doses and close monitoring for side effects.
NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnant women; acetaminophen may be selected.
In patients with diabetes, the analgesic regimen should be adjusted to avoid blood glucose fluctuations.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of dull or aching pain in the anterior knee or behind the patella, especially aggravated by going up and down stairs, squatting, and standing up after prolonged sitting ('theater sign'). Some patients have knee crepitus, clicking, or mild swelling; symptoms may be relieved by rest but recur after increased activity.

first_questions: Where exactly is your knee pain? Is it worse when going up or down stairs or squatting?
Have you recently felt knee discomfort when standing up suddenly after sitting for a long time?
Is the pain continuous, or does it occur only after exercise?
followup_questions: If you have clicking or a sensation of friction, please describe the nature and frequency of the sound.
Have you had any recent knee trauma or excessive exercise (such as running or deep squats)?
Can the pain be significantly relieved by rest or ice application?
stop_conditions: A strong association between pain and specific movements (such as going up or down stairs, squatting) has been established, and there is no history of acute trauma.
The patient has described the typical 'theater sign' and retropatellar crepitus, and signs of infection such as redness, swelling, heat, and pain have been excluded.
The history is sufficient to distinguish degenerative changes from acute injury, and further questioning about systemic symptoms is not needed.

essential: Bilateral knee X-ray (including axial patellar view)
Knee MRI
if_suspected: Musculoskeletal ultrasound (to assess patellofemoral tracking and synovial status)
Lower limb alignment and gait analysis
avoid: Routine CT scan (higher radiation and lower soft-tissue resolution than MRI)
Joint aspiration (no indication when there is no infection or obvious effusion)

first_line: First-line treatment is conservative: during the acute phase, reduce weight-bearing activities and avoid deep squatting and stair climbing.

Physical therapy includes strengthening training of the vastus medialis and iliotibial band stretching. Pharmacologically, short-term oral NSAIDs may be used (such as ibuprofen 0.2 g three times daily after meals, for no more than 2 weeks), combined with topical flurbiprofen gel patch. If necessary, a patellar strap may be used to improve loading.
safety_warnings: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with a history of peptic ulcer or severe renal insufficiency, and the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding should be watched for.
Long-term high-dose use of analgesics may mask disease progression; efficacy should be reassessed periodically.
Avoid indiscriminate high-intensity resistance training to prevent worsening cartilage wear.
personalization: In adolescent patients, the focus is on correcting poor posture and strengthening muscle strength, and surgery should be avoided prematurely.
In older patients with comorbid osteoarthritis, exercise intensity should be adjusted and glucosamine supplementation considered.
Obese patients must develop a weight-loss plan to reduce patellofemoral joint load.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of severe shoulder pain and limited movement, especially aggravated by abduction or elevation of the upper limb. The affected shoulder may appear drooped and forward, and patients often support the affected elbow with the contralateral hand. Local swelling, bruising, and crepitus may be visible, and some patients may palpate an abnormal prominence of the bone end. If neurovascular injury is present, arm numbness, weakness, or changes in skin temperature may occur.

first_questions: What was the specific mechanism of injury (e.g., falling on an outstretched hand or direct impact)?
After the injury, did you hear a bone breaking sound or feel obvious displacement?
Do you currently have numbness, tingling, or coldness in the arm?
followup_questions: If accompanied by difficulty breathing or chest pain, ask further about symptoms of pneumothorax.
If there is abnormal sensation in the hand, ask further which specific fingers are numb and how long it lasts.
Ask about a history of osteoporosis or recent long-term use of corticosteroid medications.
stop_conditions: The mechanism of injury, site of pain, and presence or absence of neurovascular compromise symptoms have been clarified.
The patient can accurately describe the position at the time of injury and the sound heard at that time.
Open wounds and emergency signs of severe complications have been excluded.

essential: Anteroposterior clavicle X-ray
Anteroposterior shoulder X-ray
if_suspected: Chest CT (when pneumothorax or pulmonary contusion is suspected)
Brachial plexus ultrasound or electromyography (when nerve injury is suspected)
Angiography (when subclavian vascular injury is suspected)
avoid: Routine whole-body bone scan (when there is no indication of multiple fractures)
Repeated X-ray examinations (unless required by clinical change or preoperative planning)
CT before blind manual reduction (when there is no evidence of complex displacement)

first_line: For nondisplaced or minimally displaced fractures, conservative treatment is preferred: immobilize the affected limb with a figure-of-eight bandage or clavicle strap for 4-6 weeks, combined with NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen 0.2 g tid) for pain and swelling. Begin early fist clenching and wrist exercises, and start passive shoulder movement after 3 weeks. For comminuted fractures, shortening of more than 2 cm, or fractures at high risk of skin pressure, open reduction and internal fixation is recommended.
safety_warnings: Avoid early large-range shoulder abduction to prevent failure of internal fixation or nonunion.
Monitor skin pressure to prevent axillary skin necrosis or brachial plexus traction injury caused by the figure-of-eight bandage.
Be alert for delayed pneumothorax, especially in fractures of the middle third with pleural injury.
personalization: Older patients with osteoporosis require longer immobilization and calcium and vitamin D supplementation.
In children with greenstick fractures, a triangular sling may be used for immobilization without strict figure-of-eight fixation.
Athletes or manual workers seeking rapid recovery may consider early surgical intervention.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of numbness and tingling on the dorsum of the foot and lateral lower leg, accompanied by foot drop (inability to dorsiflex the toes) and a steppage gait. Typically, the toe drags when walking, and the leg must be lifted high to avoid tripping. Some patients may mention recent compression or trauma to the lateral knee. Symptoms are usually unilateral; bilateral symptoms should raise suspicion of systemic disease.

first_questions: Do you feel numbness on the dorsum of your foot or the lateral lower leg? Do you have trouble lifting your foot when walking?
Have you recently had an injury to the lateral knee, prolonged cross-legged sitting, or compression from a cast?
followup_questions: Does the numbness extend to the toes? Is the pain continuous or intermittent?
Do you have diabetes, a history of alcohol abuse, or recent rapid weight loss?
stop_conditions: The sign of foot drop has been confirmed, and a clear cause of trauma or compression has been identified.
The patient can clearly describe the steppage gait and confirm the area of sensory impairment.
Symptoms related to lumbar spine disease (such as low back pain radiating to the lower limb) have been excluded.

essential: Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies (NCS)
Active ankle dorsiflexion strength examination (graded 0-5)
Pain and light touch examination of the dorsum of the foot skin
if_suspected: Knee MRI (to rule out space-occupying lesions or cysts at the fibular head)
Lumbar spine MRI (to differentiate lumbar disc herniation)
Lower limb vascular ultrasound (to exclude vascular factors)
avoid: Routine plain X-ray (unless fracture is suspected; it has no diagnostic value for the nerve itself)
Unnecessary nerve block test (may interfere with subsequent electrophysiological assessment)
Nonspecific blood tumor marker screening (when there is no indication)

first_line: During the acute phase, conservative treatment is primary: strictly avoid compression of the lateral knee and wear an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) to correct foot drop and prevent falls. Pharmacologically, give mecobalamin (0.5 mg tid) to promote nerve repair, combined with vitamin B1. Physical therapy includes nerve gliding exercises and low-frequency electrical stimulation. If there is no improvement after 3-6 months or in cases of open injury, surgical exploration for release or grafting is required.
safety_warnings: Strictly avoid prolonged knee flexion, which may cause further nerve compression.
Use corticosteroid pulse therapy with caution to avoid masking infection or worsening abnormal blood glucose.
Pay attention to foot care to prevent burns or ulcers due to sensory loss.
personalization: Patients with diabetes need stricter blood glucose control to promote nerve regeneration.
In older patients, focus on preventing falls and fractures, and strengthen the fitting of assistive devices.
Athletes should be evaluated for recovery of motor function before returning to competition.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with abnormal hand appearance or functional limitation, such as missing digits, syndactyly (webbed connection), polydactyly, thumb hypoplasia, or limited wrist movement. Infants and young children often present with weak grip, inability to perform fine motor tasks, or parents noticing asymmetric hand shape or abnormal digit alignment. Some affected children have other skeletal anomalies of the elbow or forearm, requiring comprehensive assessment combined with family history and birth history.

first_questions: Did the child have any obvious hand abnormalities at birth? What were the specific findings?
Is one hand or both hands affected? Does it affect grasping or daily activities?
Is there a family history of similar hand malformations?
followup_questions: If polydactyly or syndactyly is found, ask whether other limb or visceral anomalies are present.
If the anomaly is unilateral, ask whether pain or functional impairment has developed with age.
Ask whether any prior treatment or surgical intervention has been received.
stop_conditions: The type of malformation has been clarified and there are no other systemic symptoms.
The family fully understands the condition and expresses willingness to treat.
Necessary physical examination has been completed and the diagnostic direction is clear.

essential: Hand radiographs (PA and lateral views)
Skeletal survey radiographs
Hand ultrasonography (to assess soft tissue, vessels, and nerves)
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (preoperative planning for complex bony malformations)
Genetic testing (if syndromic malformation is suspected)
Electromyography (to assess neuromuscular function)
avoid: Routine MRI (unless soft tissue tumor or complex neuropathy is suspected)
Invasive biopsy (not needed for non-neoplastic malformations)
Repeated low-value X-rays (to avoid cumulative radiation exposure)

first_line: Select an individualized plan according to the type of malformation: for mild malformations, orthotic correction and rehabilitation training may be initiated first.

Polydactyly, syndactyly, and similar conditions require surgical excision or separation, with the optimal timing at 6-18 months. Postoperative splinting and functional exercises are used to promote hand development. Nonpharmacologic interventions include occupational therapy guidance for home care.
safety_warnings: Anesthesia risk: infants and young children require rigorous cardiopulmonary evaluation.
Infection prevention: postoperative wound care is critical.
Prevention of nerve injury: meticulous intraoperative technique is required to protect neurovascular bundles.
personalization: In preterm or low-birth-weight infants, surgery should be delayed until weight targets are met.
Patients with associated syndromes require multidisciplinary collaboration to develop a staged treatment plan.
Psychological support: provide counseling and adjustment guidance for older children.

skills.presentation: Patients often report localized sharp or dull pain at the unilateral or bilateral costosternal junctions adjacent to the sternum, and the pain may worsen with deep breathing, coughing, sneezing, or upper limb movement. The typical sign is marked localized tenderness, but there are no infection signs such as skin redness, swelling, or warmth. Pain may radiate to the back or shoulder and is easily misdiagnosed as angina or pulmonary disease; identification requires correlation with pain provoked by palpation.

first_questions: Where exactly in the chest is the pain located? Is it worsened by pressure?
Have you recently had severe coughing, heavy lifting, or chest trauma?
Is the pain related to the depth of breathing or changes in specific positions?
followup_questions: If the pain is crushing and accompanied by chest tightness and shortness of breath, ask: 'Does the pain radiate to the left shoulder or jaw? Is there sweating or nausea?'
If there is local redness and swelling, ask: 'Is the skin temperature elevated? Is there fever or a recent history of infection?'
If the pain persists without relief, ask: 'Is there also pain at rest at night? Has there been unexplained weight loss?'
stop_conditions: A localized tender point is identified and symptoms of cardiopulmonary emergencies (such as dyspnea and profuse sweating) are excluded.
Pain is confirmed to be highly related to mechanical movements (such as turning the body or raising the arm), and there are no systemic signs of infection.
The patient has clearly described the triggers (such as exercise or coughing), and vital signs are stable.

essential: Chest physical examination (with emphasis on palpation of the costochondral junctions)
Electrocardiography (ECG) to exclude myocardial ischemia
Chest X-ray (to exclude fracture and pulmonary lesions)
if_suspected: Chest CT (if occult fracture or tumor is suspected)
Inflammatory marker testing (ESR, CRP, if infectious costochondritis is suspected)
Ultrasonography (to assess local soft tissue swelling or fluid collection)
avoid: Routine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (not essential unless osteomyelitis or tumor is suspected)
Invasive needle biopsy (contraindicated when there is no evidence of infection)
Excessive reliance on radionuclide scanning (limited diagnostic value and increased radiation)

first_line: First-line treatment is nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as oral ibuprofen 400mg three times daily for a course of 1-2 weeks

Combine with local heat application and rest, and avoid triggering movements. Physical therapy such as ultrasound or transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation may help relieve symptoms. If pain is severe, local block injection of glucocorticoid combined with a local anesthetic may be considered, but strict aseptic technique is required.
safety_warnings: Contraindicated in patients with active peptic ulcer, severe renal impairment, or NSAID allergy.
Note that concomitant use of NSAIDs with anticoagulants (such as warfarin) increases bleeding risk.
Local block injection requires precautions against infection, subcutaneous fat atrophy, and glycemic fluctuations.
personalization: Use NSAIDs with caution in older adults; selective COX-2 inhibitors are recommended, with monitoring for gastrointestinal adverse effects.
NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women; acetaminophen and physical therapy are preferred.
In pediatric patients, adjust the dose by body weight and avoid aspirin to prevent Reye syndrome.

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe wrist pain, swelling, and limited movement, often accompanied by obvious deformity (such as dinner fork or bayonet deformity). After injury, the wrist cannot bear weight, and making a fist is difficult. If associated nerve injury is present, numbness or decreased sensation in the thumb and index finger may occur. Physical examination shows marked localized tenderness and positive crepitus or abnormal mobility.

first_questions: What was the specific mechanism of injury (such as falling onto an outstretched hand)?
After the injury, is there obvious wrist deformity or inability to move?
followup_questions: Do the fingers feel numb or tingly?
Did the injured area rapidly develop severe swelling or pale/purplish skin?
stop_conditions: The mechanism of injury is clear, and typical deformity and functional impairment are present.
It has been confirmed that there is no open wound or sign of severe neurovascular injury.
The patient's reported symptoms are stable, and imaging can be performed without further history-taking.

essential: Wrist radiographs (PA and lateral views)
Additional oblique X-ray view if necessary
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the wrist (to assess the degree of articular surface comminution)
Electromyography (when median nerve compression is suspected)
avoid: Blind manual reduction without prior imaging assessment
Immediate MRI in patients with suspected fracture but negative X-ray (unless occult injury is highly suspected)

first_line: For undisplaced or minimally displaced fractures, cast or splint external fixation is preferred; the fixation range usually includes the elbow to limit rotation, for a course of about 4-6 weeks. Markedly displaced or intra-articular fractures require closed reduction and percutaneous Kirschner wire fixation or open reduction and plate internal fixation. Early postoperative guidance on finger functional exercises is provided to prevent stiffness, and X-rays are repeated regularly to monitor fracture healing.
safety_warnings: Be alert for compartment syndrome; emergency management is required if severe pain or pain on passive stretch occurs.
Avoid excessively tight fixation that causes circulatory compromise; closely monitor distal perfusion.
Prolonged immobilization may cause complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), requiring early intervention.
personalization: In older patients with osteoporosis, prolong fixation time and supplement calcium and vitamin D.
In pediatric patients, protect the growth plate and avoid excessive traction that may cause growth disturbance.
For patients whose occupations require high-demand fine hand use, active surgery is recommended to achieve anatomic reduction.

skills.presentation: Patients often have a history of prolonged bed rest, limb immobilization, or paralysis and report unexplained generalized or localized bone pain, most commonly in the lower back, hips, and lower limbs. The pain is a persistent dull ache that worsens with activity or weight bearing and may be slightly relieved by rest. Some patients sustain fractures from minor trauma, presenting with sudden severe pain, deformity, and functional impairment. Muscle atrophy and joint stiffness are often present.

first_questions: Have you had a history of immobilization such as prolonged bed rest, cast fixation, or hemiplegia?
Have you recently felt persistent dull pain in the lower back, hips, or legs?
Have you recently had severe pain after a minor fall or sprain?
followup_questions: Does the pain worsen at night, and does it affect sleep?
Do you have a history of fracture or long-term use of steroid medications?
What is your current limb mobility, and is there marked muscle atrophy?
stop_conditions: The cause of immobilization is clear and the symptoms are typical; no further questioning about immobilization details is needed.
It has been confirmed that there is no recent risk of new fracture, and vital signs are stable.
The patient can clearly describe the nature of the pain and its relationship to activity, and there is sufficient information for differential diagnosis.

essential: Bone mineral density testing by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)
Measurement of serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone levels
X-ray of the affected area
if_suspected: 25-hydroxyvitamin D level testing
Urinary N-terminal telopeptide (NTX) or β-C-terminal telopeptide (β-CTX) testing
Spinal MRI (to exclude vertebral compression fracture and other lesions)
avoid: Routine CT scanning (high radiation dose and not first-line for bone density assessment)
Unnecessary whole-body bone scan (unless metastatic tumor is suspected)
Invasive bone biopsy (considered only when the cause is unclear and other bone disease is highly suspected)

first_line: The primary measure is to remove immobilization as early as possible and initiate progressive rehabilitation training to restore weight bearing. Pharmacologic treatment includes calcium supplementation (1000-1200mg daily) and vitamin D (800-1000IU daily). For high-risk patients, anti-osteoporosis drugs are needed, such as bisphosphonates (oral alendronate once weekly), usually for at least 3 years. Physical therapy should also be combined to improve muscle strength.
safety_warnings: Bisphosphonates are contraindicated in patients with severe renal impairment and esophageal disorders; after taking the medication, remain upright for 30 minutes to prevent esophageal injury.
Monitor serum calcium levels to avoid hypercalcemia, especially when active vitamin D is used concomitantly.
Be alert for the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw; dental examination is recommended before treatment.
personalization: In older patients, adjust drug doses according to renal function and prevent falls.
For long-term bedridden patients, increase the frequency of passive movement to prevent deep vein thrombosis.
In patients with diabetes, strict glycemic control is needed to promote bone healing.

skills.presentation: Patients often report recurrent joint dislocation or subluxation, accompanied by chronic polyarticular pain and easy fatigue after activity. Typical manifestations include skin hyperextensibility (e.g., slow recoil after stretching) and tissue fragility with unexplained bruising or hypertrophic scarring. Some patients describe fractures or ligament tears after minor trauma, with slow healing, often accompanied by postural abnormalities and muscle strain due to joint hypermobility.

first_questions: Have you had multiple joint dislocations or habitual sprains without obvious trauma?
Is your skin particularly soft or stretchy, or does it tend to leave wide scars?
followup_questions: Did this joint instability and skin laxity begin in childhood?
Has anyone else in your family had similar joint problems or skin features?
stop_conditions: At least 3 major clinical features (such as joint hypermobility, increased skin extensibility, family history) have been clearly confirmed.
The patient has provided sufficient past medical history to exclude other connective tissue diseases.
The symptom description is highly consistent with the typical manifestations of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and further differential diagnosis is not needed.

essential: Beighton score assessment
Whole-body skin elasticity and scar assessment
Plain radiography of affected joints
if_suspected: Echocardiography (to screen for aortic root dilation)
Ophthalmologic slit-lamp examination (to screen for lens dislocation)
Genetic testing (COL5A1/COL5A2, etc.)
avoid: Unnecessary invasive arthroscopic exploration
High-dose corticosteroid injection
Unnecessary whole-body CT scan

first_line: First-line treatment is mainly nonpharmacologic intervention, including physical therapy to strengthen core muscles and stabilize joints, and avoidance of high-impact sports. For pain management, acetaminophen or short-term NSAIDs are preferred. For patients with frequent dislocations, braces are needed for protection and instruction in correct joint movement techniques should be provided. Surgery should be considered cautiously only when conservative treatment is ineffective and function is severely affected, because the risk of postoperative healing problems is relatively high.
safety_warnings: High-dose corticosteroid injections around joints are strictly prohibited to prevent tendon rupture.
During anesthesia, special attention should be paid to airway management and difficulty with vascular puncture, and vigilance for hypotensive reactions is required.
Avoid anticoagulants for thrombosis prophylaxis unless there is a clear indication, because the bleeding risk is increased.
personalization: For pediatric patients, focus should be on joint stability training during growth and development, avoiding early weight-bearing.
For older patients, rehabilitation intensity should be adjusted, with emphasis on preventing osteoporosis and falls.
For pregnant women, pelvic girdle support should be strengthened and cardiovascular changes monitored.

skills.presentation: Patients often report numbness, tingling, or decreased sensation on the anterior thigh and medial lower leg, accompanied by knee weakness, manifesting as the knee giving way during walking and inability to actively extend the lower limb. Some patients may have quadriceps femoris atrophy and diminished or absent knee reflex. If acute trauma is present, there may be severe pain or hematoma in the inguinal region; if due to compressive injury, symptoms often worsen progressively.

first_questions: Have you recently had hip surgery, prolonged squatting/sitting, or compression in the inguinal region?
When did the numbness and weakness in your leg begin? Did they start suddenly or worsen gradually?
followup_questions: Besides the anterior thigh, do you also have numbness in the toes or dorsum of the foot?
Do you often fall because your knee suddenly gives way when walking?
stop_conditions: The sensory deficit area (anterior thigh/medial lower leg) and motor dysfunction (weak knee extension) have been clearly distinguished.
It has been confirmed whether there are clear risk factors such as trauma history, surgery history, or space-occupying lesions.
The patient can clearly describe changes in the knee reflex and specific manifestations of limitation in daily activities.

essential: Neurologic physical examination (focusing on quadriceps femoris strength and patellar tendon reflex)
Lower-limb sensory distribution map examination (L2-L4 dermatomes)
Lumbar spine MRI (to exclude compression from high lumbar disc herniation)
if_suspected: Pelvic and inguinal CT or MRI (to screen for hematoma or tumor compression)
Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction velocity studies (to localize the site and severity of injury)
Vascular ultrasound (to exclude femoral artery hematoma compression)
avoid: Routine plain radiography (limited diagnostic value for soft-tissue nerve injury)
Lumbar puncture without indication (increases infection risk and is not first-line)
Blind nerve exploration surgery (before imaging or electrophysiologic localization)

first_line: In the acute phase, conservative treatment is mainly used, including bed rest, avoidance of excessive hip flexion, NSAIDs (e.g., celecoxib 200 mg qd) to relieve pain, and mecobalamin (0.5 mg tid) to promote nerve repair. Physical therapy includes isometric quadriceps femoris contraction training and nerve gliding exercises. If caused by hematoma or tumor compression, timely surgical decompression is required. The course is usually 3-6 months, with regular EMG follow-up to assess recovery.
safety_warnings: Long-term NSAID use requires monitoring for risks of gastrointestinal bleeding and renal impairment.
Although mecobalamin has a high safety profile, rare allergic reactions should be watched for.
Avoid high-intensity resistance training while the nerve is unstable to prevent muscle strain.
personalization: Patients with diabetes need strict glycemic control to improve nerve microcirculation.
Older patients should prevent falls and use a walking aid when necessary.
Pregnant women should use NSAIDs with caution, prioritizing physical therapy and acetaminophen.

skills.presentation: Patients report pain on the volar aspect of the fingers, with obvious morning stiffness that slightly improves after activity. Typical manifestations include triggering or catching during finger flexion and extension, and in severe cases the finger can be locked in flexion and unable to extend (trigger finger). A painful nodule can be palpated locally, with increased pain on pressure, often accompanied by difficulty making a fist.

first_questions: Which finger hurts most? Do you have fingers that get stuck and cannot straighten when you wake up in the morning?
Is the pain accompanied by triggering or a 'click' sound when the finger moves?
Have you recently had work or repetitive movements requiring frequent hand use?
followup_questions: If the finger is stuck in a bent position, can it be forced straight with external force?
Does nighttime pain affect sleep? Do symptoms improve after rest?
Do you have a history of diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, or gout?
stop_conditions: The main affected finger and typical triggering/catching symptoms have been clearly identified.
It has been confirmed that there is no history of systemic joint disease and that local signs are typical.
The patient has clearly described triggers (such as overuse) and symptom duration.

essential: Physical examination: observe finger range of motion, palpate the volar aspect of the metacarpophalangeal joint for a tender nodule, and perform the Finkelstein test or passive hyperextension to provoke triggering.
High-frequency ultrasound: assess tendon sheath thickness, effusion, and tendon gliding.
if_suspected: X-ray examination: to exclude osseous lesions such as osteoarthritis or fracture.
Blood tests: if rheumatoid arthritis or gout is suspected, check ESR, C-reactive protein, and uric acid.
avoid: Routine CT scan: low soft-tissue resolution and high radiation exposure, not first-line.
Non-contrast MRI: unless complex differential diagnosis is needed, it has low cost-effectiveness for simple tenosynovitis.

first_line: First-line treatment includes immobilization and pharmacologic intervention. It is recommended to wear a brace to limit movement of the affected finger for 2-4 weeks, with oral NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 0.3 g tid or celecoxib 0.2 qd) for 7-14 days. Local heat application can promote circulation. If conservative treatment is ineffective, tendon sheath block injection (compound betamethasone + lidocaine) can be performed; it usually takes effect after 1 injection, and if necessary, it can be repeated once after 2 weeks.
safety_warnings: Never inject corticosteroids directly into the tendon to prevent tendon rupture.
Patients with diabetes need close monitoring of blood glucose fluctuations after injection.
Avoid repeated local injections within a short period to prevent skin atrophy or pigmentation.
personalization: Pregnant women should use oral NSAIDs with caution, prioritizing physical therapy and brace immobilization.
In older patients with osteoporosis, strict aseptic technique and dose control are required during injection.
Occupational manual workers need to adjust work posture and prolong the immobilization period.

skills.presentation: Patients report sudden severe pain in the upper arm, with obvious swelling, deformity, and limited movement. They often describe a 'snap' or hearing crepitus at the time of injury. The affected limb cannot be actively raised or rotated, and pain increases when the fracture site is touched. If combined with radial nerve injury, wrist drop and numbness in the dorsal first web space may occur.

first_questions: What was the specific mechanism of injury? Was there direct blunt trauma or a fall from height?
Did arm deformity or inability to move occur immediately after the injury?
Do you have numbness or abnormal sensation in the fingers?
followup_questions: If you have numbness in your hand, which specific area has decreased sensation? Can you actively raise your thumb and wrist?
If you have an open wound, how deep is it? Is there ongoing bleeding or retained foreign material?
Do you have a history of osteoporosis or long-term use of corticosteroid medications?
stop_conditions: The injury mechanism, symptom characteristics, and initial neurovascular assessment results have been clearly established.
The patient has undergone X-ray examination and the imaging results clearly show the fracture type.
Open fracture and the risk of severe vascular injury have been excluded.

essential: Anteroposterior and lateral X-ray views of the humerus
Upper-limb neurovascular function examination (focusing on the radial nerve)
Complete blood count and coagulation function tests
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (for preoperative planning of complex comminuted fractures)
Electromyography (when delayed radial nerve injury is suspected)
Vascular ultrasound (when concomitant vascular injury is suspected)
avoid: Blind manual reduction attempts (before imaging assessment)
Unnecessary whole-body MRI (unless pathologic fracture is suspected)
Repeated X-ray exposure (when there is no clinical indication)

first_line: Closed stable fractures are preferably treated conservatively: immobilization with a U-shaped cast or functional brace, maintaining the elbow at 90 degrees of flexion, and slinging the affected limb. X-rays are repeated every 2 weeks to adjust the fixation position; the course is about 8-12 weeks. Open fractures or those with obvious displacement require emergency surgery with open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), commonly using plate and screws or an intramedullary nail. Early postoperative non-weight-bearing exercises of the fingers and shoulder and elbow joints are performed to prevent stiffness.
safety_warnings: Be alert for compartment syndrome; if severe swelling pain or pain on passive stretch occurs, immediate decompression is required.
When anticoagulants are used, monitor bleeding risk and avoid worsening hematoma compression of the nerve.
During immobilization, closely observe distal perfusion to prevent ischemic necrosis caused by overly tight bandaging.
personalization: Older patients with osteoporosis should have prolonged immobilization and receive calcium and vitamin D supplementation.
Pediatric patients are mostly treated conservatively, with attention to growth plate protection and avoidance of excessive traction.
Patients with bilateral fractures or polytrauma require priority management of life-threatening injuries and staged treatment.

skills.presentation: Patients often report lateral knee pain, which worsens especially after downhill running, descending stairs, or prolonged walking. The pain is fixed at the lateral femoral epicondyle and may be accompanied by localized friction or snapping. It resolves with rest but tends to recur with resumed activity. Some patients describe tightness on the lateral thigh, with marked pain on palpation.

first_questions: At which specific movements is the pain on the outside of your knee most obvious?
Have you recently increased your running distance or frequency, or changed your training surface?
followup_questions: Does the pain radiate to the lateral thigh or lower leg?
Does the pain completely disappear after a few days of rest?
stop_conditions: A clear strong correlation between pain and specific athletic movements (e.g., push-off, downhill running) has been established
No history of intra-articular knee structural injury (e.g., meniscal tear) has been confirmed
The patient can accurately point to the tender point at the lateral femoral epicondyle

essential: Ober's test
Adductor muscle tightness assessment
Lateral knee tenderness examination
if_suspected: Knee MRI (to rule out meniscal or ligament injury)
Lower limb alignment and gait analysis
Pelvic X-ray (to screen for hip joint pathology)
avoid: Routine whole-knee CT scan (unless fracture is suspected)
Unnecessary intra-articular aspiration
Non-targeted systemic blood inflammatory marker screening

first_line: First-line treatment is conservative: in the acute phase, strict immobilization and ice application to the affected area for 15-20 minutes, 3 times daily

Oral NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 400 mg, 3 times daily, taken after meals, course no more than 7 days). Combine with physical therapy for iliotibial band stretching and gluteus medius strengthening. Adjust running form, avoid downhill running, and use orthotic insoles if needed to correct excessive foot inversion.
safety_warnings: Long-term high-dose NSAID use requires vigilance for gastrointestinal bleeding risk
Avoid forced high-intensity stretching before pain resolves, which may cause tearing
If redness, swelling, heat, and pain worsen, stop the drug immediately and seek medical care to rule out infection
personalization: Elderly patients should use NSAIDs cautiously; topical patches or physical therapy are recommended instead
Athletes need a gradual return-to-sport plan to prevent recurrence
Patients with flatfoot must have customized orthotic insoles to improve biomechanics

skills.presentation: Patients report joint swelling, a feeling of fullness, or heaviness, with limited range of motion.
