On examination, the joint contour is obliterated, and the patellar ballottement test is positive (for the knee); local skin temperature may be elevated, but skin color is usually normal. Pain is often present, worsening especially with weight-bearing or flexion-extension activity, and some patients may palpate fluctuation.

first_questions: Which joint is swollen? How long has it lasted?
Have you had recent trauma or excessive exercise?
Are there other systemic symptoms such as fever, morning stiffness, or rash?
followup_questions: If the joint is red, swollen, hot, and painful, ask: Is the pain sharp or dull? Does it worsen at night?
If there is trauma, ask: Did you hear a pop at the time of injury? Were you able to continue walking then?
If the course is chronic, ask: Do you have a history of gout, rheumatoid arthritis, or tuberculosis?
stop_conditions: Acute unilateral joint swelling has been clearly identified without signs of systemic infection, initially judged as traumatic or degenerative disease.
Polyarticular involvement with typical autoimmune disease features (e.g., morning stiffness >1 hour) has been confirmed.
The patient has already undergone arthrocentesis or imaging, and the diagnostic direction is clear.

essential: Joint ultrasound (to assess effusion volume and synovial thickness)
Plain X-ray (to rule out fracture, osteoarthritis, or bone destruction)
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein/erythrocyte sedimentation rate (to differentiate infectious from noninfectious inflammation)
if_suspected: Synovial fluid analysis (cell count, crystal examination, bacterial culture)
MRI (to assess meniscal or ligament injury and bone marrow edema)
Autoantibody panel (e.g., RF, anti-CCP antibodies to screen for rheumatoid arthritis)
avoid: CT scanning before fracture is excluded (increased radiation and inferior soft tissue resolution compared with MRI)
Blind steroid injection therapy without first excluding septic arthritis
Whole-body PET-CT without indication (too costly and not first-line)

first_line: The primary management is etiologic treatment and symptomatic relief. In the acute phase, strict immobilization, ice application, and elevation of the affected limb. For pharmacotherapy, first-line NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 0.4 g tid or celecoxib 200 mg qd), course 3-7 days. If a large effusion impairs function, arthrocentesis may be performed with injection of a small amount of glucocorticoid (e.g., triamcinolone acetonide 10-20 mg), but strict aseptic technique is required. Combine with physical therapy to promote absorption.
safety_warnings: Do not inject glucocorticoids into the joint cavity when septic arthritis is suspected, to avoid worsening infection spread.
Long-term NSAID use requires monitoring for gastrointestinal bleeding risk and changes in renal function; use cautiously in elderly patients.
Repeated arthrocentesis may cause articular cartilage injury or secondary infection; frequency should be controlled.
personalization: Elderly patients should preferentially receive selective COX-2 inhibitors to reduce gastrointestinal side effects.
NSAIDs and steroids are contraindicated in pregnant women; physical therapy and brace immobilization alone are recommended.
Patients with gouty arthritis need combined urate-lowering therapy (e.g., febuxostat), not anti-inflammatory treatment alone.

skills.presentation: Patients often report symmetric pain and stiffness in limb joints (especially fingers, toes, knees, and ankles), most prominent in the morning. As the disease progresses, limited joint mobility and deformities develop (e.g., “short fingers,” “claw hand”), accompanied by muscle atrophy. Children may show short stature and abnormal gait. Symptoms are chronic and progressively worsening, mostly occurring in low-selenium areas, without systemic signs of infection such as fever.

first_questions: Have you lived for a long time in northwestern China or high-cold mountainous areas?
Are the joints of your fingers or toes deformed or shortened?
Do your knees or ankles often hurt and feel difficult to move when walking?
followup_questions: Is the joint pain worst when you get up in the morning, and does it ease after activity?
Are there family members with similar joint deformities or short stature?
Have you had recent trauma or exposure to other factors that may cause joint damage?
stop_conditions: The patient has been confirmed to live in the endemic area and has typical joint deformity manifestations.
Imaging has shown characteristic bone-end changes.
Other common joint diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and tuberculosis have been excluded.

essential: Plain X-ray of both hands and both feet
Plain X-ray of the knees and ankles
Serum selenium level testing
if_suspected: Whole-spine plain X-ray (to assess height development and vertebral morphology)
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody testing (to differentiate rheumatoid arthritis)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein (to rule out inflammatory disease)
avoid: Unnecessary CT scanning (unless complex preoperative planning is needed)
Bone marrow aspiration (not a hematologic disease)
Synovial fluid bacterial culture (when there is no evidence of infection)

first_line: Early-stage treatment is mainly nonpharmacologic, including selenium supplementation (oral sodium selenite, 0.1-0.2 mg daily, course 3-6 months), nutritional improvement, and moderate functional exercise. In the middle and late stages, for severe joint deformity, physical therapy may be considered to relieve pain. If severe joint dysfunction or deformity is present, orthopedic surgery or arthroplasty is required. Avoid excessive weight-bearing to prevent worsening of the disease.
safety_warnings: Strictly monitor the selenium supplementation dose; overdose can cause toxicity (hair loss, nail deformity, neurological damage).
Use selenium-containing preparations cautiously in patients with renal insufficiency, and adjust the dose.
Surgical patients need coagulation function assessment to prevent postoperative infection and thrombosis.
personalization: For pediatric patients, the selenium dose must be precisely calculated according to body weight, and growth and development indicators should be monitored.
For elderly patients with osteoporosis, combined calcium and vitamin D supplementation should be given.
For patients disabled by severe joint deformity, minimally invasive surgical approaches with less trauma and faster recovery should be preferred.

skills.presentation: Patients often report sudden catching or locking of the joint, limited range of motion, and severe pain. Symptoms are mostly intermittent; a sudden “stuck” sensation occurs during movement and may resolve after changing position. Some patients may palpate a mobile intra-articular mass, accompanied by swelling and crepitus.

first_questions: Has your joint ever suddenly caught or been unable to move?
Is this catching accompanied by severe pain or swelling?
followup_questions: Does the catching occur after specific movements?
Have you had a history of trauma or long-term joint wear?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes typical catching and locking symptoms
A history of trauma or degenerative joint disease has been confirmed
The frequency of symptoms and triggers are clear

essential: Plain X-ray examination
MRI magnetic resonance imaging
if_suspected: CT three-dimensional reconstruction
Arthroscopy
avoid: Routine blood tests (unless infection is suspected)
Ultrasound without indication

first_line: First-line treatment includes conservative treatment and surgical treatment. Conservative treatment is suitable for patients with mild symptoms, using NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 400 mg, 3 times daily) to relieve pain, combined with physical therapy to improve joint function. If symptoms are frequent or severely affect daily life, surgical removal of the loose body is required, commonly using arthroscopic minimally invasive technique. Postoperative rehabilitation training should last 4-6 weeks.
safety_warnings: Avoid anticoagulant drugs to prevent intraoperative bleeding
Note that NSAIDs may cause gastrointestinal reactions
Postoperatively, be alert for infection risk
personalization: Elderly patients need osteoporosis assessment to adjust the treatment plan
Pediatric patients need cautious selection of surgical timing
Patients with concomitant arthritis need combined antirheumatic treatment

skills.presentation: The patient reports obvious abnormal limb appearance, such as angular, rotational, or shortening deformity. It is often accompanied by persistent pain, limited joint range of motion, and functional impairment, with symptoms worsening on weight-bearing. Some patients may develop compensatory strain of adjacent joints, leading to abnormal gait or muscle atrophy. The history often includes a clear trauma history and improper reduction and fixation.

first_questions: How soon after the injury did you notice the limb deformity? Was reduction and fixation performed at that time?
Do you currently have persistent pain or limited movement in the affected limb? Which specific movements make it worse?
followup_questions: Do you have symptoms of neurovascular compression such as numbness, weakness, or decreased sensation?
During previous treatment, did any internal fixation loosening, breakage, or wound infection occur?
stop_conditions: The deformity type (angular/rotational/shortening) and time of onset have been clarified.
The degree of major functional impairment and associated neurovascular symptoms have been established.
The previous treatment course and current imaging findings have been confirmed.

essential: Full-length anteroposterior and lateral X-rays of the affected limb (including adjacent joints)
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (to assess callus morphology and joint surface status)
if_suspected: Lower-limb alignment measurement and analysis (to assess biomechanical changes)
Electromyography (when concomitant nerve injury is suspected)
avoid: Whole-body bone scan without indication
Unnecessary soft-tissue MRI (unless deep infection or tumor is suspected)

first_line: Surgical correction is the mainstay, including osteotomy, internal fixation reconstruction, and bone grafting. Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is selected according to the site of deformity, with external fixation as needed. Postoperative early functional exercise and physical therapy are required to prevent joint stiffness. The treatment course depends on bone healing and usually requires follow-up for 3-6 months until bony union.
safety_warnings: Strictly assess the position of the neurovascular bundle to avoid secondary intraoperative injury.
Pay attention to anticoagulation therapy to prevent deep vein thrombosis, especially in older patients.
Be alert to the risk of postoperative infection; standardized antibiotic use and aseptic technique are required.
personalization: In pediatric patients, consider the effect on the growth plate and avoid overcorrection that may impede growth.
For patients with osteoporosis, use reinforced internal fixation or combine it with bone cement augmentation.
For older patients or those with multiple comorbidities, minimally invasive techniques should be used to reduce surgical stress.

skills.presentation: The patient often reports medial elbow pain, especially aggravated by making a fist, lifting heavy objects, or forearm supination. The pain may radiate to the forearm and is accompanied by local tenderness and limited movement. Some patients describe it as persistent dull pain and may also feel discomfort at night while resting.

first_questions: Where exactly is your elbow pain located?
Is the pain aggravated by specific movements (such as lifting heavy objects)?
followup_questions: Is the pain accompanied by numbness or weakness?
Have you had any elbow trauma or a history of repetitive strain?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described typical symptoms and has no other complex medical history.
The pain has been confirmed to be related to specific movements, with no signs of nerve compression.
The patient understands the preliminary diagnosis and agrees to further examination.

essential: Physical examination: medial elbow tenderness test
Imaging: plain X-ray (to rule out fracture or other lesions)
if_suspected: Ultrasound (to assess the degree of tendon injury)
MRI (when severe tendon tear is suspected)
avoid: CT scan (unless complex fracture is suspected)
Unnecessary blood tests (e.g., if there are no signs of infection)

first_line: First-line treatment includes rest, ice application, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., ibuprofen 400mg three times daily for 1-2 weeks). Physical therapy can help restore function, and a brace may be used to immobilize the elbow and reduce movement if necessary.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term NSAID use to prevent the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
Note the drug allergy history; in particular, NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with aspirin allergy.
If severe pain or worsening swelling occurs, stop the drug immediately and seek medical care.
personalization: Older patients should have reduced NSAID doses and renal function monitoring.
Pregnant women should choose safe medications under medical guidance.
Athletes may require a longer rehabilitation period and an individualized training plan.

skills.presentation: The patient reports persistent numbness, burning, or prickling pain on the anterolateral thigh, usually confined to a band-like area from the anterior superior iliac spine to above the knee joint. Symptoms are often aggravated by standing, walking, or wearing tight clothing, and relieved by rest or lying flat. On examination, reduced or hypersensitive tactile sensation may be found in this area, but there is no muscle weakness or reflex abnormality, and the knee jerk reflex is normal.

first_questions: Where exactly on your thigh is the pain or numbness? Is it distributed in a band-like pattern?
Recently, have you worn a tight belt or abdominal binder, or had a significant weight gain?
How long after standing or walking do symptoms worsen, and do they improve when you lie down?
followup_questions: Besides numbness and pain, do you have weakness or muscle atrophy in the leg?
Are the symptoms unilateral or bilateral? Is your sleep affected at night?
Have you had recent abdominal surgery or a history of lumbar spine disease?
stop_conditions: It has been clarified that symptoms are confined to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve distribution and there is no motor impairment.
Triggers (such as tight clothing or obesity) have been confirmed, and typical manifestations of lumbar spine disease have been excluded.
The symptoms described by the patient are highly consistent with the signs, and no further inquiry about systemic symptoms is needed.

essential: Physical examination: lateral femoral cutaneous nerve percussion test and sensory threshold testing
Lumbar MRI: to rule out radiating pain caused by lumbar disc herniation
Electromyography (EMG): to assess lateral femoral cutaneous nerve conduction function
if_suspected: Pelvic X-ray: to screen for pelvic fracture or compression by abnormal bony structures
Blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin testing: to rule out diabetic peripheral neuropathy
High-resolution ultrasound: to locate the nerve compression point and assess surrounding soft tissue
avoid: Unnecessary lumbar puncture: this disease is not a central nervous system infection or inflammation
Routine whole-spine CT: in the absence of clear trauma or indications of complex low back pain
Empirical use of strong opioids: lacking evidence and associated with high risk

first_line: Conservative treatment is preferred, including avoiding tight clothing, weight reduction, and physical therapy. Pharmacologically, first-line options are gabapentin (starting at 100mg at night, gradually titrated to 300-900mg/day) or pregabalin (75mg bid), with a 2-4 week course to observe efficacy. If local pain is severe, local block injection at the nerve exit (lidocaine combined with a small amount of corticosteroid) may be considered.
safety_warnings: Gabapentin/pregabalin require vigilance for central depressant effects such as dizziness and somnolence; use with caution when driving.
Corticosteroid injection requires strict aseptic technique to prevent local infection and subcutaneous fat atrophy.
Long-term high-dose use of antiepileptic analgesics requires monitoring of liver and kidney function and complete blood count.
personalization: Pregnant women: prioritize physical therapy; drug use should balance fetal safety and avoid teratogenic risk.
Older adults: start at half the dose, titrate slowly, and prevent fall risk.
Patients with diabetes: strictly control blood glucose and differentiate diabetic neuropathy from compression syndrome.

skills.disease: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome)

skills.presentation: The patient often reports a tearing-like severe pain at the affected site during exercise or a sudden movement, immediately followed by local weakness. Typical manifestations include rapid swelling at the injured site and subcutaneous bruising; on palpation, a marked tender point or a depression in the muscle belly may be felt. Pain is aggravated by active contraction of the affected muscle and is also felt on passive stretching; in severe cases, limited joint movement and abnormal gait may occur.

first_questions: What specific movement were you doing when you were injured? Did you hear any sound at that time?
Where is the pain most severe now? Can you point to it precisely with your finger?
followup_questions: Immediately after the injury, were you unable to continue activity or walking?
Is there obvious local swelling or skin discoloration (bruising)?
Have you had similar injuries or a history of chronic pain at this site before?
stop_conditions: The injury mechanism, pain characteristics, and degree of functional limitation have been clarified.
It has been confirmed that there is no open wound or sign of neurovascular injury.
The patient can clearly describe the timeline of injury and initial management measures.

essential: Physical examination: inspect for swelling and bruising, palpate to locate tenderness and defects, and assess active/passive range of motion.
Ultrasound: dynamically assess muscle fiber continuity, extent of hematoma, and grading.
Plain X-ray: to rule out associated fracture or avulsion injury.
if_suspected: MRI: used to evaluate severe strain, complete rupture, or complex soft-tissue injury.
Electromyography: if concomitant nerve compression or neurogenic injury is suspected.
avoid: Heat application or deep massage during the acute phase (within 24-48 hours).
Blind resistance strength testing that may aggravate the injury.
CT scanning without indication (soft-tissue resolution is inferior to MRI and radiation exposure is high).

first_line: Follow the RICE principle: rest and immobilization, ice application (15-20 minutes each time, 3-4 times daily), compression bandaging, and elevation of the affected limb. Pharmacologically, early oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., ibuprofen 0.2g three times daily) relieve pain and inflammation
During the later stage, physical therapy is combined to promote repair. Mild strains usually require 1-2 weeks of rest, while moderate to severe strains require 4-6 weeks of rehabilitation training.
safety_warnings: Contraindicated or use with caution in patients allergic to NSAIDs or with a history of peptic ulcer disease.
Avoid topical ointments that promote blood circulation and remove blood stasis during the acute bleeding phase.
Be alert to the risk of deep vein thrombosis; monitor lower-limb symptoms during prolonged immobilization.
personalization: Older patients require reduced-dose NSAIDs and renal function monitoring.
Athletes need a staged return-to-sport plan to prevent re-rupture.
Patients with diabetes need strict blood glucose control to promote soft-tissue healing.

skills.presentation: Patients often develop progressive local swelling, pain, and limited joint mobility weeks to months after trauma or surgery. Palpation may reveal induration within the muscle, which gradually hardens like bone over time; skin temperature may be elevated. The typical presentation is stiffness and functional impairment at the injured site after the recovery period, with severe pain provoked by passive joint movement, and symptoms progressively worsen.

first_questions: When and how did your injury or surgery occur?
Has a new lump or increased hardness developed at that site in recent weeks?
followup_questions: Does the pain worsen at night or affect your sleep?
Has your joint range of motion decreased significantly compared with the early period after the injury?
stop_conditions: A history of trauma is established and typical symptoms of progressive ossification are present
Imaging has confirmed heterotopic ossification
The patient's complaints are highly consistent with the physical signs, with no confounding systemic disease

essential: Plain X-ray (to assess ossification maturity)
Dual-energy CT (to assess ossification volume and density)
Alkaline phosphatase testing (to help determine the active phase of ossification)
if_suspected: MRI (to differentiate soft tissue infection or tumor)
Bone scan (for early detection of metabolically active lesions)
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (to rule out infection)
avoid: Blind open biopsy (may induce spread of inflammation)
Excessive massage or forceful passive stretching (worsens ossification)
Steroid pulse therapy before infection has been ruled out

first_line: In the acute phase, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., indomethacin 25mg tid for 6-8 weeks) are the mainstay for preventing progression of ossification, combined with physical therapy to maintain joint range of motion while avoiding forceful stretching. If ossification is mature (usually requiring 12-18 months) and severely affects function, surgical excision of heterotopic bone tissue may be performed. Postoperatively, radiotherapy or medication is needed to prevent recurrence.
safety_warnings: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with peptic ulcer disease or a bleeding tendency
Long-term high-dose indomethacin requires monitoring of renal function and gastrointestinal reactions
During radiotherapy, surrounding normal tissues must be strictly protected to prevent radiation injury
personalization: Older patients require reduced-dose NSAIDs and enhanced gastrointestinal protection
Patients with spinal cord injury should start prophylactic pharmacotherapy as early as possible
Pediatric patients should use steroid drugs with caution, with physical interventions preferred

skills.presentation: Patients often report recurrent swelling, pain, and limited mobility of a joint (most commonly the knee), especially worsening after exercise. A typical feature is a sensation of 'locking' or 'catching' within the joint; in some patients, a loose body in the joint can be palpated, causing sudden inability to extend or flex. Symptoms occur intermittently and may be relieved by rest, but as the disease progresses, pain becomes continuous and is accompanied by marked joint effusion and clicking.

first_questions: Does your joint pain worsen significantly after strenuous exercise or weight-bearing?
Recently, have you felt your joint getting stuck and unable to move, or suddenly clicking?
followup_questions: If catching occurs, can you restore movement by moving the joint yourself? How long does it last?
Have you had recurrent swelling or fluid accumulation in the joint?
stop_conditions: Pain is clearly related to exercise and typical joint locking symptoms are present.
A history of similar trauma or a family predisposition has been confirmed.
The patient has described mechanical obstruction caused by an intra-articular loose body.

essential: Plain X-ray of the knee (AP and lateral views and axial patellar view)
Knee MRI
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (to assess the extent of bone defect and location of loose bodies)
Arthroscopy (for diagnosis and assessment of cartilage stability)
avoid: Routine ultrasound (limited diagnostic value for osteochondral lesions)
Radionuclide bone scan without an indication

first_line: For early, nondisplaced lesions, conservative treatment is preferred, including strict immobilization (brace fixation for 4-6 weeks), avoidance of weight-bearing, and NSAIDs for pain relief. If the lesion is unstable or has detached to form a loose body, arthroscopic drilling, microfracture, or osteochondral transplantation is required. Postoperative rehabilitation training is combined to gradually restore joint range of motion and muscle strength; the course usually takes 3-6 months.
safety_warnings: Strenuous exercise or weight-bearing is strictly prohibited during the acute phase to prevent further detachment of the lesion.
NSAID use requires attention to the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding; use with caution in older adults.
Surgical procedures require precise localization to avoid injury to adjacent blood vessels, nerves, and normal cartilage.
personalization: Adolescent patients with open growth plates should first be considered for knee-preserving reparative surgery.
Older patients with severe osteoarthritis may require joint replacement rather than simple repair.
Athletes require a staged return-to-play plan to prevent recurrence.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with recurrent fractures after minor trauma, accompanied by skeletal deformities (such as scoliosis and long-bone bowing). Some patients have blue sclerae, hearing loss, and abnormal tooth development. Infants and young children are prone to multiple fractures, whereas adults may have chronic pain or limited mobility due to increased bone fragility.

first_questions: Have you had a history of recurrent fractures?
Does anyone in your family have similar symptoms?
followup_questions: Were the fractures caused by minor trauma?
Do you have blue sclerae or hearing problems?
stop_conditions: Multiple fractures after minor trauma are established and the family history is positive
Typical signs such as blue sclerae and hearing loss have been confirmed
Imaging shows significantly reduced bone density

essential: Whole-body X-ray examination
Bone density measurement
Genetic testing (COL1A1/COL1A2)
if_suspected: Head CT to assess skull morphology
Hearing test
Dental examination
avoid: Unnecessary radionuclide scanning
Bone marrow aspiration without an indication
Overreliance on MRI for diagnosis

first_line: First-line treatment includes bisphosphonates (e.g., pamidronate disodium, with the dose adjusted according to age), given by intravenous injection once weekly for 6-12 months. Physical therapy is also recommended to strengthen muscle strength and balance and reduce the risk of falls. For severe cases, surgical fixation of the fracture site may be considered.
safety_warnings: Bisphosphonates may cause hypocalcemia; serum calcium levels should be monitored
Avoid concomitant use with aluminum-containing drugs to prevent worsening renal toxicity
Long-term use may lead to osteonecrosis of the jaw; regular oral examinations are required
personalization: Pediatric patients require dose adjustment according to body weight
Bisphosphonates should be used with caution in pregnant women, with nonpharmacologic interventions preferred
Older patients should have renal function assessed before medication

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe localized persistent pain, accompanied by redness, swelling, warmth, pain, and functional impairment. The acute phase often includes systemic toxic symptoms such as high fever and chills; the chronic phase may show a wound that does not heal for a long time, recurrent purulent discharge, or sinus tract formation, and sometimes a bony prominence can be palpated or sequestrum may be discharged. Pain worsens at night or with activity, local skin temperature is elevated, and tenderness is marked.

first_questions: Have you recently had trauma, surgery, or underlying diseases such as diabetes?
Is the painful area accompanied by redness, swelling, warmth, or fever?
Is there purulent discharge from the wound or a wound that has not healed for a long time?
followup_questions: If you have had fever, what was the highest temperature, and how many days did it last?
If there is a wound, what is the color of the discharge, and is there a foul odor?
Have you recently had sepsis or a distant infection focus?
stop_conditions: Local redness, swelling, warmth, and pain with systemic infection symptoms are established, and the history is clear
An open wound with purulent discharge and signs of bone destruction has been confirmed
The patient has clear high-risk factors (such as diabetic foot) and typical local signs are present

essential: Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (CRP)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Plain X-ray of the affected site
if_suspected: MRI (to assess bone marrow edema and soft tissue abscess)
Bacterial culture and drug susceptibility testing (aspirate or drainage fluid)
CT scan (to observe sequestrum formation and details of bone destruction)
avoid: Unnecessary weight-bearing activity before fracture has been ruled out
Blind incision and drainage without imaging localization
Prophylactic systemic antibiotic use without an indication

first_line: In the acute phase, intravenous infusion of susceptible antibiotics is preferred, usually for 4-6 weeks, adjusted according to susceptibility results. This should be combined with debridement surgery to remove necrotic bone tissue and drain abscesses. In the chronic phase, thorough excision of sequestrum and bone grafting for repair are required. Adjunctive measures include immobilization and elevation of the affected limb, nutritional support, and control of underlying diseases such as blood glucose.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of aminoglycosides, which can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity
Be aware that quinolones may carry a risk of tendon rupture
Watch for antibiotic-associated diarrhea and superinfection
personalization: Patients with diabetes require strict glycemic control to improve microcirculation
Pediatric patients require attention to the risk of growth plate injury and dose adjustment
Patients with renal insufficiency require antibiotic dose adjustment according to creatinine clearance

skills.presentation: Patients often report deep, dull pain in the hip or knee. Initially, it worsens after activity and relieves with rest; as the disease progresses, persistent pain and night pain occur. Typical signs are limited range of motion of the affected limb, especially severe pain provoked by internal rotation and abduction, and some patients have a limp. If the femoral head is involved, groin tenderness and radiating pain to the medial thigh may occur; in advanced stages, muscle atrophy and joint deformity may be seen.

first_questions: Where exactly is the pain located? Is it constant or does it occur only with activity?
Have you recently had long-term use of corticosteroid medications or a history of heavy alcohol consumption?
Have you ever had trauma to the hip or knee (such as a fracture or dislocation)?
followup_questions: Does the pain radiate to the medial thigh or knee?
Has your walking distance been significantly shortened because of the pain?
Do you also feel pain at rest at night that affects your sleep?
stop_conditions: The nature of the pain, triggers, and associated symptoms have been clarified, and traumatic and nontraumatic factors can be distinguished.
The patient has provided a complete medication history (especially glucocorticoids) and information on lifestyle habits.
The lesion site and severity have been preliminarily assessed, sufficient to determine the imaging examination plan.

essential: Plain X-ray of both hips (AP and frog-leg views)
MRI of the affected joint (magnetic resonance imaging)
Complete blood count and coagulation function tests
if_suspected: CT scan (to assess the degree of bone collapse and cystic changes)
Bone density measurement (to screen for comorbid osteoporosis)
Full lipid panel and autoantibody screening (to differentiate metabolic or immune causes)
avoid: Radionuclide bone scan without an indication (less valuable for early diagnosis than MRI)
Routine joint aspiration biopsy (unless infection or tumor is suspected)
Repeated low-dose X-ray examinations (increase radiation exposure and are insensitive to early necrosis)

first_line: For early asymptomatic or mildly painful disease, conservative treatment is preferred, including strict weight-bearing restriction (use of crutches), physical therapy, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as celecoxib 0.2g bid). For high-risk populations, anticoagulation or lipid-lowering drugs may be considered. In intermediate-to-advanced stages or when collapse occurs, surgical intervention is required, such as core decompression combined with bone grafting, or artificial joint replacement. The treatment course depends on staging; follow-up is usually required for 6-12 months to assess efficacy.
safety_warnings: Long-term high-dose glucocorticoid use can worsen osteonecrosis; it must be strictly monitored and tapered gradually.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may cause gastrointestinal bleeding; older patients should receive concomitant gastric mucosal protectants.
Surgical implants carry a risk of infection; blood glucose should be controlled before surgery and prophylactic antibiotics should be used.
personalization: For adolescent patients, hip-preserving surgery is preferred to preserve joint function.
For older adults or those with severe underlying diseases, total hip arthroplasty is recommended rather than complex reconstruction.
Pregnant women should avoid contrast-enhanced MRI and certain anticoagulants; the treatment plan should be adjusted.

skills.presentation: Patients report severe anterior knee pain, with marked swelling and subcutaneous ecchymosis. The typical presentation is inability to actively extend the knee (extensor mechanism disruption), difficulty walking, or complete inability to bear weight. On examination, an abnormal patellar contour and significant local tenderness are seen; if crepitus is palpable or a fracture gap can be palpated, a comminuted fracture is suggested. Some patients have an open wound.

first_questions: What was the exact mechanism of injury? (e.g., direct impact, fall onto the knees)
After the injury, can you actively lift your lower leg or straighten your knee?
Did the knee swell rapidly and develop bruising?
followup_questions: If you cannot straighten it, is it due to sudden weakness or severe continuous pain that makes you afraid to move?
Is there any break in the skin with bleeding?
Do you have a history of osteoporosis or long-term corticosteroid use?
stop_conditions: Inability to extend the knee has been clearly described, and there is local crepitus or deformity
An open wound requiring emergency management has been confirmed
Symptoms and signs are highly consistent, and there is no need to ask further about nonspecific pain details

essential: AP and lateral knee X-ray
Axial patellar X-ray
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the knee (to assess the degree of comminution and articular surface congruity)
MRI (when concomitant meniscal or ligament injury is suspected)
avoid: Blind forceful passive knee flexion-extension testing (may worsen the injury)
Applying heat or massage before fracture has been excluded
Refusing imaging confirmation based only on physical examination

first_line: For patients without displacement and with an intact extensor mechanism: immobilization in a cast or brace in the extended position for 4-6 weeks; knee flexion is prohibited during this period, and progressive isometric quadriceps contraction exercises are started. For patients with displacement (>2mm) or extensor dysfunction: emergency open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is required, commonly with tension-band wire or screw fixation. Passive motion should begin early after surgery to prevent joint adhesions.
safety_warnings: Do not forcefully flex the knee during the acute phase, to prevent further separation of fracture fragments
Monitor distal perfusion and sensation of the affected limb, and watch for compartment syndrome
Postoperative deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis is required; high-risk patients should receive anticoagulants
personalization: For older patients with osteoporosis: consider cannulated screws combined with wires or special locking plates to enhance purchase
For severe comminuted fractures: if the articular surface cannot be reconstructed, consider partial or total patellectomy
For patients with diabetes: strictly control blood glucose to prevent wound infection and delayed healing

skills.presentation: Patients report anterior knee pain localized to the inferior pole of the patella or the patellar tendon insertion. Typically, pain worsens with jumping, squatting, stair climbing, or rising after prolonged sitting, and relieves with rest. On examination, marked local tenderness is present, sometimes with mild swelling, but there is usually no joint effusion or limitation of movement. The pain follows a chronic course, lasting weeks to months, and morning stiffness may be present.

first_questions: Where exactly is the pain located in the front of the knee?
Which movements (such as jumping or squatting) trigger or worsen the pain?
How long have the symptoms lasted, and have you had any history of acute injury?
followup_questions: If the pain worsens after exercise, how long does it take to relieve with rest?
Do you have rest pain at night that affects sleep?
Has your training volume or exercise intensity increased suddenly recently?
stop_conditions: The pain has been clearly localized to the patellar tendon insertion and is load-related
Typical symptoms of an intra-articular loose body or meniscal injury have been excluded
The patient's exercise habits and recent changes in load have been understood

essential: Knee physical examination (with focus on palpation of the patellar tendon and inferior pole of the patella)
Ultrasound examination (to assess tendon thickness, echogenicity, and blood flow signal)
Plain X-ray (to exclude bony lesions or calcification)
if_suspected: MRI (when partial tendon tear or severe degeneration is suspected)
Dynamic musculoskeletal ultrasound (to assess tendon gliding)
avoid: Routine joint aspiration (unless infection or crystalline arthritis is suspected)
Blind CT scanning (higher radiation and lower soft-tissue resolution than MRI)

first_line: Conservative treatment is preferred, including relative immobilization to reduce triggering movements, combined with eccentric strength training (such as decline board squats). For pharmacotherapy, short-term nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as ibuprofen 400mg three times daily for no more than 2 weeks) may be used to control acute inflammation. Physical therapy such as shockwave therapy is effective for chronic cases. The treatment course is usually 3-6 months, with gradual progression of load.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term, frequent corticosteroid injections to prevent the risk of tendon rupture
Monitor for gastrointestinal adverse effects and renal function with NSAIDs
Do not perform forceful high-intensity eccentric training during acute severe pain
personalization: For older patients, pay attention to osteoporosis and adjust the intensity of weight-bearing training
For athletes, develop a staged rehabilitation plan according to the competition season
For patients with diabetes, strictly control blood glucose to promote tissue repair

skills.presentation: Patients often report inward depression of the sternum and costal cartilages, forming a funnel-shaped deformity. It is most common in adolescents, with visible depression in the center of the anterior chest wall. Some patients have decreased exercise tolerance, easy fatigue, palpitations, or chest tightness, especially after strenuous activity. Severe cases may have shortness of breath or recurrent respiratory infections; diagnosis requires combined assessment of appearance and symptoms.

first_questions: When did you first notice the chest depression?
Do you usually feel short of breath, palpitations, or chest pain during exercise?
followup_questions: Has the degree of depression worsened with age?
Is there any similar chest wall deformity in your family?
stop_conditions: The depression morphology has been clarified and there are no symptoms of cardiopulmonary compression
The past medical history and family history have been obtained
The patient has clearly expressed their willingness regarding surgery

essential: Three-dimensional chest CT reconstruction
Echocardiography
Pulmonary function tests
if_suspected: Electrocardiogram (to screen for arrhythmia)
Spine X-ray (to exclude concomitant scoliosis)
avoid: Routine chest X-ray (limited value for deformity assessment)
MRI without an indication

first_line: For mild asymptomatic cases, observation and follow-up are the main approach, with regular monitoring of chest wall development

For moderate-to-severe cases with cardiopulmonary compression or psychological distress, Nuss procedure correction is preferred. After surgery, a chest binder should be worn for 3-6 months, with respiratory training and pain management. Nonpharmacologic interventions include posture correction and core muscle exercises, but they cannot reverse the skeletal deformity.
safety_warnings: Before surgery, coagulopathy and active infection must be excluded
Be alert to the intraoperative risk of puncturing the pericardium or major vessels
Postoperatively, watch for plate displacement and pneumothorax complications
personalization: For pediatric patients, minimally invasive procedures are preferred to reduce effects on growth
For older patients, assess the degree of osteoporosis and adjust the fixation strategy
For patients with connective tissue diseases such as Marfan syndrome, multidisciplinary joint evaluation is required

skills.presentation: Patients often report recurrent swelling and pain in a single joint (most commonly the knee), which may be intermittent or persistent. The typical presentation is limited joint motion with a sensation of catching or locking. On examination, diffuse joint swelling is seen, and skin temperature may be mildly elevated, but skin color is usually normal. Patients with a longer disease course may develop muscle atrophy, and some have a history of trauma; symptoms are easily misdiagnosed as meniscal injury or rheumatoid arthritis.

first_questions: How long have your joint pain and swelling lasted? Are they persistent or do they come and go?
Do you feel that the joint catches and cannot move, or does it suddenly click?
Have you had any joint sprain or trauma recently?
followup_questions: Does the swelling improve after resting overnight, or is it swollen all day?
Besides pain, do you feel a sensation of something rubbing inside the joint or hear clicking?
Have you had joint aspiration before, and was the fluid reddish or brownish?
stop_conditions: Recurrent monoarticular swelling and pain with locking symptoms have been clearly established, and signs of acute infection have been excluded.
The patient has described typical intermittent swelling and mechanical catching symptoms.
Previous tests suggest abnormal synovial fluid properties, and further imaging confirmation is needed.

essential: X-ray plain film (to assess bone erosion and soft tissue swelling)
MRI (gold standard for diagnosis, showing synovial thickening and characteristic hemosiderin deposition)
Synovial fluid analysis (to differentiate hemorrhagic from noninflammatory effusion)
if_suspected: CT scan (to assess the extent of bone erosion and for preoperative planning)
Whole-body bone scan (to screen for multiple lesions or metastatic tumors)
Coagulation function tests (to exclude joint hemarthrosis caused by hematologic disorders)
avoid: Routine full rheumatology antibody panel (unless rheumatoid arthritis is suspected)
Arthroscopic exploration without indication (confirmation by MRI should be obtained first)
Repeated diagnostic joint aspiration (increases infection risk and is unnecessary)

first_line: Surgery is the first-line treatment, including arthroscopic synovectomy or open surgical resection to completely remove the diseased synovial tissue. Postoperative rehabilitation training is used to restore joint function. For patients who cannot tolerate surgery or have multiple recurrences, radionuclide therapy (e.g., yttrium-90) may be considered. Drug therapy is only adjunctive; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are used to relieve pain, and no specific drug can cure this disease.
safety_warnings: Surgery requires vigilance for injury to adjacent neurovascular structures, especially in the popliteal fossa.
Postoperatively, deep vein thrombosis must be prevented, especially in elderly patients or those with prolonged immobilization.
Avoid early weight-bearing, which may cause intra-articular bleeding or implant loosening (if replacement surgery is performed).
personalization: In pediatric patients, the growth plate should be preserved as much as possible, and minimally invasive arthroscopic techniques should be used to reduce physeal injury.
In elderly patients with osteoporosis, intraoperative manipulation should be gentle to prevent iatrogenic fracture.
For patients with multiple joint involvement, staged surgery should be performed, prioritizing the most symptomatic joint and strengthening nutritional support.

skills.presentation: Patients report an abnormal increase in the number of fingers or toes, often with an extra digit on the thumb or little finger side. Some children have nail hypoplasia, bifurcated phalanges, or limited joint motion. Parents may describe it as 'my child has six fingers' or 'the toes are fused together.' If associated with a syndrome, systemic symptoms such as cardiac murmur, renal abnormalities, or intellectual developmental delay may be present.

first_questions: Is the extra digit unilateral or bilateral?
Was it present at birth, and has it enlarged or become infected recently?
Is there any family history of similar cases?
followup_questions: If abnormalities in other areas are present, ask: 'Does the child have a cardiac murmur or difficulty urinating?'
If a syndrome is suspected, ask: 'Are the child's motor development and intelligence consistent with those of peers?'
Ask whether the child has previously received local treatment or bandaging.
stop_conditions: The type and extent of the deformity have been clearly established, and there are no signs of a systemic syndrome.
Imaging studies have been completed, and a surgical plan can be formulated.
The parents understand the timing of surgery and prognosis and agree to follow-up.

essential: X-ray plain film of the affected limb (AP and lateral views)
Physical examination (to assess soft tissue coverage and neurovascular course)
if_suspected: Whole-body skeletal X-ray screening (to exclude multiple malformations)
Echocardiography (to screen for congenital heart disease)
Abdominal ultrasound (to screen for renal abnormalities)
avoid: Routine CT scan (high radiation and insufficient soft tissue resolution)
MRI (not first-line unless complex neurovascular involvement is present)
Unnecessary genetic testing (when there are no clear indications of a syndrome)

first_line: Surgery is the first-line treatment, usually performed at 6-18 months of age. Procedures include excision of the extra digit, reconstruction of joint ligaments and tendons, and epiphyseal fixation when necessary. Postoperatively, plaster immobilization is required for 3-4 weeks, along with functional exercises. For simple soft-tissue polydactyly, early ligation may be considered, but blood supply must be strictly evaluated.
safety_warnings: Avoid injury to the median nerve and major vascular branches.
Be alert to the risk of postoperative infection and wound dehiscence.
Contraindicated in patients with uncorrected coagulopathy.
personalization: Surgery should be delayed in premature or low-birth-weight infants until weight is adequate.
Patients with associated syndromes require multidisciplinary consultation to develop a staged plan.
For bilateral deformities, simultaneous or staged early correction is recommended to improve function.

skills.presentation: Patients often have a clear history of joint trauma (such as fracture or ligament injury), and persistent joint pain develops months or years after the injury, worsening with activity and relieved by rest. The typical presentation includes morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes, accompanied by joint swelling, a sensation of friction, and limited motion. Some patients have joint deformity or recurrent effusion, and symptoms progressively worsen, affecting daily walking or weight-bearing function.

first_questions: What was the exact time and mechanism of your injury? Did you undergo surgery or reduction at that time?
With which movements is the pain most obvious now? Does it completely relieve with rest?
Has the joint ever been repeatedly swollen or felt 'stuck'?
followup_questions: If the pain worsens with weather changes or on rainy days, please describe how severe it is.
Recently, has the joint suddenly been unable to straighten or bend?
Have you previously received rehabilitation or injections for this joint? How effective were they?
stop_conditions: The history of trauma is clear and symptoms are consistent with typical features of post-traumatic osteoarthritis; no further history is needed.
The patient has provided complete imaging reports sufficient to assess joint space and bone changes.
The relationship between pain characteristics and activity is clear, and there are no warning symptoms such as nerve compression.

essential: Weight-bearing X-ray plain film of the affected limb (to assess joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation)
MRI (to assess cartilage injury, meniscal and ligament residual lesions)
Physical examination: measurement of joint range of motion and localization of tender points
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (to assess malunion after complex fractures)
Synovial fluid aspiration analysis (to exclude infection or crystal arthritis)
Full-length lower-limb alignment X-ray (to assess mechanical axis deviation)
avoid: Routine whole-body bone scan (unless multiple metastases or occult fracture is suspected)
Unnecessary arthrography (replaced by MRI and increases trauma risk)
Non-weight-bearing X-ray as the main diagnostic basis (cannot reflect the true loading state)

first_line: First-line treatment is conservative: oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., celecoxib 200 mg/day for 2-4 weeks) combined with physical therapy (hot compresses, muscle strength training). If pain is severe, intra-articular sodium hyaluronate injection may be given (once weekly for 3-5 consecutive doses). At the same time, reduce weight-bearing, use a brace for support, and control body weight to reduce joint load.
safety_warnings: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with a history of gastrointestinal ulcer or severe renal insufficiency, and a gastric mucosal protective agent should be used concomitantly.
Glucocorticoid injections should not exceed 3 times per year to avoid inducing infection or accelerating cartilage destruction.
Long-term NSAID use requires monitoring of liver and kidney function and cardiovascular risk.
personalization: For elderly patients, topical NSAIDs are preferred to reduce systemic side effects.
Obese patients must have a weight-loss plan; otherwise, drug efficacy is limited.
For young, active patients in whom conservative treatment fails, early arthroscopic debridement or osteotomy should be considered rather than total joint replacement.

skills.presentation: Patients report severe shoulder pain and limited motion, often triggered by a fall onto an outstretched hand or direct impact to the shoulder. The typical presentation is swelling and deformity of the affected upper arm, marked local tenderness, and limitation of both active and passive shoulder motion. Some patients may have upper-limb numbness, suggesting possible neurovascular injury. In elderly patients with osteoporosis, minor trauma can cause fracture, and occult injury should be suspected.

first_questions: What was the exact mechanism of injury (e.g., fall position, direction of force)?
Did severe shoulder pain and inability to raise the arm occur immediately after the injury?
followup_questions: Do you have numbness, tingling, or decreased sensation in the fingers?
Do you have a history of osteoporosis or long-term use of glucocorticoids?
stop_conditions: The injury mechanism is clear and symptoms are typical, with no signs of neurovascular injury.
The patient has undergone imaging and received a diagnosis; no further history is needed.
The patient's vital signs are stable, pain score is controllable, and there is no indication for emergency surgery.

essential: AP X-ray of the proximal humerus
Y-view X-ray of the proximal humerus
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (for assessment of complex fractures)
if_suspected: Shoulder MRI (if concomitant rotator cuff tear is suspected)
Vascular ultrasound (if axillary artery injury is suspected)
Electromyography (if brachial plexus injury is suspected)
avoid: Blind shoulder reduction maneuvers (before imaging confirmation)
Repeated unnecessary whole-body CT scans (increase radiation and provide no benefit)
Joint aspiration without excluding contraindications

first_line: Nonoperative treatment is suitable for undisplaced or minimally displaced fractures: sling immobilization for 3-4 weeks with early pendulum exercises to prevent frozen shoulder. Surgical treatment is suitable for obvious displacement, multi-segment fractures, or fractures with dislocation; locking plate internal fixation or shoulder hemiarthroplasty is preferred. Postoperatively, a progressive rehabilitation plan should be developed according to fracture stability, with active motion usually started at 6-8 weeks.
safety_warnings: Violent traction of the affected limb is strictly prohibited to prevent secondary neurovascular injury.
Anticoagulant drugs should be used cautiously to prevent deep vein thrombosis while avoiding bleeding risk.
Prolonged immobilization requires prevention of shoulder stiffness and disuse osteoporosis.
personalization: For elderly patients with osteoporosis, minimally invasive fixation or joint replacement should be prioritized to reduce complications.
For young patients with high-energy injuries, anatomic reduction should be pursued to restore function.
For patients with diabetes, blood glucose must be strictly controlled to promote wound healing.

skills.presentation: Patients typically report wrist drop (drop wrist) and inability to actively extend the elbow, wrist, and fingers. It is often accompanied by numbness or decreased sensation in the skin on the radial aspect of the dorsum of the hand (dorsum of the thumb, index finger, and proximal phalanx of the middle finger). If the lesion is more proximal, weakness of the triceps brachii may be present, causing impaired elbow extension. Symptoms usually appear acutely after trauma or compression and are progressively worsening or persistently unresolved.

first_questions: When did the injury happen, and what caused it?
Are you currently unable to lift your hand or make a fist?
Do you have numbness in the area of the thumb on the back of your hand?
followup_questions: Before the injury, was there any history of prolonged pressure on the arm (e.g., due to alcohol intoxication or coma)?
Does the pain radiate to the lateral forearm or upper arm?
Do you have a history of diabetes or peripheral neuropathy?
stop_conditions: The injury mechanism has been clarified and the signs are typical (wrist drop + numbness in the first web space).
The patient has clearly described the extent of sensory loss and degree of motor impairment.
Similar symptoms caused by cervical spine disease have been excluded.

essential: Physical examination: assess wrist extension, finger extension, and thumb abduction
Electrodiagnostic testing (electromyography/nerve conduction velocity)
Upper limb plain radiography (to rule out compression from fracture)
if_suspected: High-resolution ultrasound (to assess nerve continuity)
MRI (to assess soft tissue compression or neuroma)
CT angiography (when concomitant vascular injury is suspected)
avoid: Routine lumbar puncture (no relevant indication)
Unnecessary whole-body PET-CT
Repeated low-value X-ray examinations

first_line: First-line conservative treatment consists of neurotrophic drugs (e.g., mecobalamin 0.5 mg tid for 3 months) and physical rehabilitation training, including passive joint mobilization to prevent contracture. For closed contusions, strict immobilization in a functional position for 4–6 weeks is required, with periodic follow-up electromyography. For open injuries or clear compression, early surgical exploration with neurolysis/repair should be performed, followed by postoperative brace fixation.
safety_warnings: Avoid prolonged excessive traction on the injured nerve, which may cause secondary injury
When using corticosteroid drugs, be alert to blood glucose fluctuations and infection risk
Monitor for drug-induced liver and kidney dysfunction
personalization: Patients with diabetes need strict glycemic control to promote nerve repair
Older patients need enhanced fall prevention education to prevent fractures
Pediatric patients need rehabilitation intensity adjusted according to growth and development

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe sharp localized chest wall pain, which is significantly exacerbated by deep breathing, coughing, or turning the body. Typical signs include distinct tenderness on palpation over the fracture site, and crepitus or abnormal mobility may be palpable. If pneumothorax or hemothorax is present, dyspnea, cyanosis, or shock may occur. Some patients avoid breathing because of pain, resulting in shallow rapid breathing.

first_questions: What was the exact mechanism of injury (e.g., impact, crush)?
Where exactly is the pain most severe?
Do you have difficulty breathing or coughing up blood?
followup_questions: Does the pain become unbearable when you take a deep breath or cough?
After the injury, have you had any brief loss of consciousness or fainting?
Do you have a history of osteoporosis or coagulopathy?
stop_conditions: The injury mechanism and pain site have been clarified, and vital signs are stable.
Serious complications (e.g., tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax) have been excluded.
The patient can cooperate with the necessary physical examination.

essential: Chest plain radiography (posteroanterior and lateral views)
Chest CT scan (three-dimensional reconstruction preferred)
Arterial blood gas analysis
if_suspected: Bedside ultrasound (FAST) to evaluate for pleural effusion
Electrocardiography (to rule out cardiac contusion)
Complete blood count and coagulation profile
avoid: Routine whole-body bone scan (unless multiple pathologic fractures are suspected)
Unnecessary needle biopsy in patients with suspected pneumothorax
Overreliance on MRI (limited value and time-consuming for cortical bone fractures)

first_line: The core management is analgesia and pulmonary rehabilitation. Multimodal analgesia is preferred, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen 400 mg q8h) combined with regional nerve block. Encourage early deep breathing exercises and effective coughing to prevent pulmonary infection. Avoid tight chest binder fixation because it may restrict respiratory movement. For flail chest or severe displacement, surgical internal fixation should be considered. The course usually takes 6–8 weeks until clinical healing.
safety_warnings: Strictly avoid excessive opioid use, which can cause respiratory depression
Be aware of the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding associated with NSAIDs
Watch for delayed hemothorax or pneumothorax
personalization: Older patients with osteoporosis need calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and fall risk should be assessed
Use potent analgesics with caution in pediatric patients, with priority given to physical therapy
Pregnant women should avoid NSAIDs; acetaminophen may be selected

skills.presentation: Patients often report persistent dull shoulder pain that worsens at night and affects sleep. Typical manifestations include increased pain when raising or abducting the arm (painful arc), accompanied by weakness, such as difficulty combing hair or dressing. Some patients have a history of trauma or long-term overuse. On physical examination, active range of motion is limited while passive range of motion is normal, and marked tenderness occurs at specific angles.

first_questions: Where exactly is the pain in your shoulder? Does it radiate to the lateral upper arm?
Which movements trigger the pain or weakness? Do you ever wake up at night because of pain?
Have you recently had any injury such as lifting heavy objects, falling, or throwing?
followup_questions: If night pain is mentioned, ask whether you have difficulty turning over in bed or need to prop up your head with pillows.
If weakness is present, ask whether you can perform fine movements such as combing your hair or fastening undergarments.
Ask whether you have a history of cervical spondylosis or diabetes to rule out referred pain.
stop_conditions: Pain is clearly related to specific movements and is accompanied by typical weakness symptoms
It has been confirmed that there are no features of radicular pain due to nerve root compression
The history is sufficient to distinguish acute trauma from chronic overuse

essential: Shoulder plain radiography (to rule out fracture and osteoarthritis)
Shoulder MRI (to confirm the degree of tendon tear and edema)
Physical examination: Neer sign, Hawkins sign, and empty can test
if_suspected: Shoulder ultrasound (dynamic assessment of tendon gliding and effusion)
CT arthrography (for complex tears or when MRI is contraindicated)
Electromyography (to differentiate shoulder pain caused by cervical spine disease)
avoid: Routine whole-spine CT (unnecessary in the absence of radicular symptoms)
Repeated resistance strength testing (may worsen the tear)
Unnecessary radionuclide scanning

first_line: Conservative treatment is preferred: oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., celecoxib 200 mg once daily for 2–4 weeks), combined with local ice application and physical therapy (ultrasound, electrical therapy). Emphasis should be placed on rotator cuff muscle strengthening training and range-of-motion exercises. If conservative treatment is ineffective after 3 months or there is a full-thickness tear, surgical repair is recommended.
safety_warnings: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with peptic ulcer disease or renal insufficiency
Avoid long-term corticosteroid injection to prevent tendon rupture
Postoperative rehabilitation must strictly follow a stepwise progression to prevent retear
personalization: In older patients, osteoporosis should be assessed and rehabilitation intensity adjusted
Patients with diabetes need strict glycemic control to promote tissue healing
Athletes need an individualized return-to-play plan based on sports demands

skills.presentation: Patients often report persistent dull pain deep in the lower back or buttocks, with pronounced morning stiffness (>30 minutes) that improves after activity. Pain may radiate to the posterior thigh but usually does not extend below the knee. Nocturnal awakening due to pain is a typical feature, and pain worsens with prolonged sitting or turning over in bed. Some patients have alternating buttock pain, in which pain alternates between the left and right buttocks.

first_questions: How long have you had pain in your lower back and buttocks? Do you feel stiff when getting up in the morning, and does it improve after activity?
Does the pain alternate (e.g., left side today, right side tomorrow)?
Do you wake up at night because of pain while resting?
followup_questions: If you have eye redness, pain, or blurred vision, please describe in detail when it occurs.
Do you have a history of psoriatic rash or chronic diarrhea?
Is there any family history of ankylosing spondylitis or other autoimmune diseases?
stop_conditions: Symptoms have been clearly established to be consistent with inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness >30 minutes, improvement with activity, worsening at rest).
It has been confirmed that there is no history of acute trauma, and emergency manifestations such as infectious fever have been excluded.
Key accompanying symptom information (eyes, skin, intestines) and family history have been obtained.

essential: Anteroposterior pelvic radiography (to assess sacroiliac joint space narrowing, sclerosis, or fusion)
Serum C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) testing
HLA-B27 genotyping
if_suspected: Sacroiliac joint MRI (T2 fat-suppressed sequence, for early detection of bone marrow edema)
Rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-CCP antibodies (to rule out rheumatoid arthritis)
Serum uric acid measurement (to rule out gouty arthritis)
avoid: Routine noncontrast lumbar CT (not first-line; high radiation and insensitive to early sacroiliac lesions)
Blind sacroiliac joint needle biopsy (unless pyogenic infection is highly suspected)
Repeated X-ray examinations (low value for early diagnosis and increased radiation exposure)

first_line: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are preferred, such as celecoxib 200 mg once or twice daily or etoricoxib 60–90 mg once daily, used continuously for at least 4 weeks to assess efficacy. Combine with physical therapy, including core muscle exercises, posture correction, and warm compresses. If NSAIDs are ineffective, refer to rheumatology to consider biologic agents (e.g., TNF-α inhibitors).
safety_warnings: Patients with a history of peptic ulcer should receive concomitant proton pump inhibitors to prevent bleeding
Avoid concomitant use with anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin) or ACEI antihypertensives to prevent kidney injury
Be alert to cardiovascular risk; long-term use requires monitoring of blood pressure and cardiac function
personalization: In older adults, selective COX-2 inhibitors are preferred to reduce gastrointestinal side effects
NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnant women; acetaminophen or specific biologic agents should be used under medical supervision
In patients with renal insufficiency, adjust the dose according to creatinine clearance or avoid use

skills.presentation: Patients complain of severe shoulder pain and limited mobility, often accompanied by local swelling, bruising, and bony crepitus. Typical manifestations are inability to abduct or raise the upper limb, with pain worsening on shoulder movement. If associated with nerve injury, numbness or weakness of the arm may occur; if the thorax is involved, dyspnea may accompany. A history of trauma (e.g., fall from height, motor vehicle accident) is an important clue to identification.

first_questions: What exactly happened at the time of injury? Was there a direct impact or fall?
Where is the pain most severe now? Can you raise your arm?
Do you have numbness, tingling, or weakness in your fingers or arm?
followup_questions: If there is chest pain or shortness of breath, ask: 'Do you feel severe chest pain when taking a deep breath or coughing?'
If nerve injury is suspected, ask: 'Has your hand grip strength decreased? Are there areas of abnormal sensation?'
Ask about past medical history: 'Do you have osteoporosis or long-term use of steroid medications?'
stop_conditions: The trauma mechanism is clear and symptoms are typical; no further detailed questioning is needed.
The patient has clearly described the extent of pain and degree of functional impairment.
It has been confirmed that there is no life-threatening associated injury (e.g., pneumothorax, massive hemorrhage).

essential: Plain X-ray of the scapula (AP and axillary views)
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the scapula
Physical examination: shoulder range of motion and neurovascular assessment
if_suspected: Chest CT (to rule out rib fracture or pneumothorax)
Brachial plexus electromyography (when nerve injury is suspected)
Angiography (when subclavian vascular injury is suspected)
avoid: Routine MRI (unless severe soft tissue tear is highly suspected and would affect surgical decision-making)
Repeated low-dose X-rays (to avoid cumulative radiation)
Blind shoulder reduction (before fracture type is clarified)

first_line: Most undisplaced fractures are managed conservatively: use a sling to suspend the affected limb for 4-6 weeks, and start pendulum exercises early to prevent stiffness. For pain management, NSAIDs are first-line (e.g., ibuprofen 0.2g tid); short-term weak opioids may be used if necessary. For comminuted fractures, marked displacement, or fractures associated with acromioclavicular joint dislocation, open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) is required, followed by postoperative rehabilitation training.
safety_warnings: Forceful large-amplitude passive shoulder movement during the acute phase is contraindicated to prevent fracture displacement.
Patients using anticoagulants should be alerted to the risk of postoperative bleeding, and coagulation function should be monitored.
Long-term bedridden patients should be protected against deep vein thrombosis; early ankle pump exercises are recommended.
personalization: Older patients with osteoporosis should receive calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and immobilization time should be prolonged.
Athletes or manual laborers need an intensified postoperative rehabilitation plan to restore function.
Patients with diabetes need strict glycemic control to promote wound healing.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of severe shoulder pain and limited mobility, with the affected limb held in abduction and elastic fixation. Typical signs include a squared-off shoulder deformity (prominent acromion) and a positive Dugas sign, i.e., when the elbow of the affected side is brought close to the chest wall, the hand cannot reach the opposite shoulder. It is mostly caused by trauma or a fall; vigilance is needed for associated greater tuberosity fracture of the humerus or sensory abnormalities in the deltoid region caused by axillary nerve injury.

first_questions: What was the exact mechanism of injury? Was there a direct impact or a history of excessive arm abduction?
Is the affected limb completely immobile at present? Can you describe the exact location of the pain?
followup_questions: Do you have numbness or weakness in your fingers? (to evaluate for neurovascular injury)
Have you had similar dislocation episodes or a history of habitual dislocation in the past?
stop_conditions: The trauma history is clear and typical squared-off shoulder deformity and positive Dugas sign are present
It has been confirmed that there is no open wound or distal limb perfusion impairment
The patient's vital signs are stable, and emergency resuscitation is not required

essential: AP and axillary X-ray views of the shoulder (to confirm dislocation direction and exclude fracture)
Physical examination: Dugas test and visual inspection for squared-off shoulder deformity
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the shoulder (to evaluate complex fractures or difficult reduction)
MRI (when associated rotator cuff tear or labral injury is suspected)
avoid: Blind forceful manual reduction before imaging
Routine use of ultrasound as the first-line diagnostic tool (poor visualization of bony structures)

first_line: Under adequate analgesia (e.g., intra-articular lidocaine injection or intravenous sedation), perform reduction using traction-countertraction or the Kocher method. After successful reduction, suspend the affected limb in a sling for 3-4 weeks for immobilization, with ice application to reduce swelling. Start pendulum exercises early to prevent frozen shoulder, and gradually restore active range of motion later.
safety_warnings: Forceful reduction is strictly prohibited to prevent iatrogenic humeral neck fracture or brachial plexus injury
After reduction, X-ray must be repeated to confirm good joint alignment and no new fracture
Observe distal limb perfusion and sensation of the affected limb, and be alert for axillary artery injury
personalization: Older patients should be evaluated for osteoporosis; reduction maneuvers should be gentle and occult fractures should be ruled out
For young athletes with a first dislocation, assess the risk of labral injury and consider surgical repair if necessary
Use anticoagulants with caution in patients with coagulation disorders to avoid hematoma formation after reduction

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of sudden swelling, elevated skin temperature, and severe pain in the affected hand, described as burning or prickling. Symptoms usually begin after stroke or upper limb fracture, manifesting as finger stiffness and limited mobility, and the skin may become shiny and desquamated. Typical signs include marked dorsal hand edema with pitting on pressure, pain exacerbated by wrist extension, and some patients have referred shoulder pain, severely affecting daily grasping function.

first_questions: When did the swelling and pain in your hand start? Have you had a stroke or arm injury before?
What is the nature of the pain? Is it continuous or worse with activity? Do you feel that the skin is hot?
followup_questions: If early inflammation is suspected, ask: 'Is it difficult to fully make a fist or straighten your fingers? Has the skin color changed to red or purple?'
If the course is prolonged, ask: 'Is there muscle wasting in the hand? Has the joint range of motion gradually decreased, causing stiffness?'
stop_conditions: The trigger (e.g., stroke, trauma) is clear and symptoms match the typical redness, swelling, heat, and pain presentation.
The degree of hand mobility limitation and the impact of pain on daily life have been confirmed.
Infectious factors (e.g., cellulitis) and typical signs of deep vein thrombosis have been excluded.

essential: Bilateral upper limb circumference measurement (to compare edema severity)
Plain X-ray (to rule out fracture and osteoporosis)
Physical examination (tenderness testing, passive extension test)
if_suspected: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density measurement (to assess osteoporosis)
Electromyography and nerve conduction velocity studies (to differentiate nerve injury)
Ultrasound (to exclude deep vein thrombosis and soft tissue fluid collection)
avoid: Unnecessary radionuclide scanning (unless the diagnosis is unclear and complex cases need to be differentiated)
Invasive joint aspiration (avoid when there is no evidence of infection)
Overreliance on CT (limited diagnostic value for soft tissue edema and higher radiation exposure)

first_line: First-line treatment includes elevating the affected limb and alternating cold compresses with warm water baths to reduce edema, along with gentle passive and active exercises to prevent stiffness. For medication, NSAIDs are preferred (e.g., celecoxib 200mg once daily), for a course of 2-4 weeks

In severe cases, short-term glucocorticoid pulse therapy may be used. At the same time, wearing a brace is recommended to limit abnormal movement, combined with rehabilitation physical therapy for sensory re-education.
safety_warnings: Long-term NSAID use requires monitoring for gastrointestinal bleeding risk and renal function; use with caution in older adults.
Glucocorticoid therapy requires strict monitoring of blood glucose fluctuations and blood pressure, and vigilance for secondary infection.
Avoid excessive massage or forceful stretching to prevent fracture or worsening of inflammation.
personalization: Older patients should receive lower NSAID doses, with topical formulations preferred to reduce systemic side effects.
Patients with diabetes require close blood glucose monitoring, adjustment of glucocorticoid dosage, and prevention of hyperglycemic crisis.
Patients with severe osteoporosis should avoid weight-bearing training and increase calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of persistent dull pain in the lower back and limb joints, limited mobility, and numbness or stiffness of the limbs. Typical manifestations include spinal rigidity and kyphotic deformity; in severe cases, lower limb weakness, difficulty walking, and even paraplegia may occur. Some patients have a history of long-term consumption of high-fluoride water or high-fluoride food, and the skin may show hyperpigmentation or depigmentation. Symptoms are chronic and progressive and are easily misdiagnosed as lumbar disc herniation or rheumatoid arthritis.

first_questions: Do you have a history of long-term consumption of well water or high-fluoride food (e.g., grain dried over coal smoke)?
How long have you had low back and leg pain, and is it accompanied by limb numbness or weakness?
followup_questions: Does the pain worsen at night or affect sleep?
Recently, have you noticed decreased height, kyphosis, or markedly limited joint mobility?
stop_conditions: A history of high-fluoride exposure is clear and typical skeletal deformity and symptoms of nerve compression are present
Imaging has confirmed features of osteosclerosis or ligament calcification
The patient cannot provide an adequate history but clinical signs are highly suggestive and referral to a specialist for evaluation is needed

essential: Plain X-ray of the entire spine
Serum fluoride concentration measurement
Urine fluoride concentration measurement
if_suspected: Lumbar CT scan (to assess the degree of spinal canal stenosis)
Electromyography (to differentiate the nature of nerve injury)
Bone mineral density testing
avoid: Unnecessary radionuclide bone scan (unless associated tumor is suspected)
Routine full rheumatology/immunology panel (when there are no specific indications)
Repeated high-dose X-ray examinations

first_line: The primary measure is to remove the source of fluoride and stop intake of high-fluoride water and food. For pharmacotherapy, NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 0.4g three times daily) are used to relieve pain, combined with vitamin D and calcium supplements to promote metabolism. In severe cases, calcium disodium edetate may be considered for defluoridation therapy, with the course determined by the condition. Physical therapy includes warm compresses, massage, and functional exercises to prevent muscle atrophy and joint stiffness.
safety_warnings: Defluoridation drugs may cause gastrointestinal reactions and renal impairment; liver and kidney function should be monitored
Avoid long-term high-dose glucocorticoids to prevent worsening of osteoporosis
Be aware of gastrointestinal irritation from NSAIDs, and use gastric mucosal protectants if necessary
personalization: In pediatric patients, the dosage of defluoridation drugs must be strictly controlled to prevent effects on skeletal development
Use anticoagulants with caution in older patients to prevent fracture risk from falls
