For patients with renal impairment, adjust the defluoridation regimen and prioritize conservative treatment

skills.presentation: Patients often present with lumbosacral skin abnormalities, such as a tuft of hair, hyperpigmentation, or dimpling. In occult spina bifida, there may be no symptoms; in manifest cases, a cystic mass on the back (meningocele or myelomeningocele) may be seen, accompanied by lower-limb motor impairment, sensory loss, urinary and fecal incontinence, or foot deformity. Infants and young children may show abnormal gait or recurrent urinary tract infections.

first_questions: At birth, was there a bulge or skin abnormality on the back?
Does the child currently have difficulty walking or fall easily?
Is there difficulty urinating, urinary incontinence, or constipation?
followup_questions: If a mass is found, ask further: Does the size of the mass change with crying? Is there ulceration or fluid drainage?
If neurologic symptoms are present, ask further: Are the symptoms progressively worsening or stable? Is there pain?
If urinary problems are suspected, ask further: Is there a history of recurrent urinary tract infections or increased nocturia?
stop_conditions: The nature of the back mass and any associated neurologic deficits have been clarified
The presence and severity of bowel and bladder dysfunction have been confirmed
A complete birth history and records of prior surgery/treatment have been obtained

essential: Lumbar spine X-ray
Spine MRI
Neurologic physical examination
if_suspected: Urinary system ultrasound
Urodynamic testing
Electromyography
avoid: Routine noncontrast CT (unless emergency to rule out fracture)
Invasive intraspinal puncture (when not indicated)

first_line: Surgical treatment is first-line, including excision of the sac, repositioning the spinal cord, and dural repair, with lamina reduction and fixation if necessary. Long-term rehabilitation training is needed after surgery to improve motor function. For patients with hydrocephalus, shunt surgery is required. Nonpharmacologic interventions include physical therapy, orthotic assistance, and bladder management training. The duration of treatment depends on the condition, and lifelong follow-up is usually required.
safety_warnings: Strictly assess infection risk before surgery and avoid operating in areas of local infection
Be aware of interactions between antiepileptic drugs and anesthetics
Watch for serious postoperative complications such as cerebrospinal fluid leakage and intracranial infection
personalization: Infants and young children should undergo surgery as early as possible to prevent worsening of neurologic damage
Adult patients require an individualized rehabilitation plan based on residual neurologic function
In patients with hydrocephalus, increased intracranial pressure should be managed first

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of persistent pain on the thumb side of the wrist (at the radial styloid), which worsens when making a fist, lifting objects, or wringing a towel. Some patients can palpate a local induration or friction sensation, and in severe cases thumb movement is limited. The typical sign is a positive Finkelstein test, in which severe pain is provoked by flexing the thumb into the palm and deviating the wrist toward the ulnar side. Symptoms are usually chronic and progressive, with marked morning stiffness; they may ease somewhat with rest but recur after exertion.

first_questions: Where is your wrist most painful? Is it concentrated at the base of the thumb?
Which movements clearly worsen the pain? For example, wringing a towel or holding a child?
followup_questions: Is the pain continuous or intermittent? Do you feel wrist stiffness when waking in the morning?
Have you recently frequently used a mobile phone, held an infant, or performed repetitive hand work?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes pain at the radial styloid and has a positive Finkelstein test; a preliminary diagnosis can be made without further questioning.
History of trauma such as fracture or dislocation and features of systemic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis have been excluded.
Symptoms have lasted more than 2 weeks and conservative treatment has been ineffective, requiring progression to the examination stage.

essential: Physical examination: Finkelstein test (fist and ulnar deviation test)
Palpation: assessment of tenderness at the radial styloid and subcutaneous nodularity
if_suspected: High-frequency ultrasound: to assess tendon sheath thickening, fluid, and tendon gliding
Plain X-ray: to rule out osteoarthritis, fracture, or osteophyte formation
avoid: Routine MRI: limited diagnostic value for simple tenosynovitis and excessively high cost
Radionuclide scanning: nonspecific and not recommended as first-line

first_line: First-line treatment includes immobilization and pharmacologic intervention. A splint is recommended to limit thumb movement for 2-4 weeks

Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., ibuprofen 0.2g three times daily after meals for 1-2 weeks). Local corticosteroid injection (e.g., compound betamethasone 1ml + lidocaine 1ml) once weekly, up to 2 times. Combine with physical therapy such as ultrasound and warm compresses to promote resolution of inflammation.
safety_warnings: Use corticosteroid injections with caution in patients with diabetes, as they may cause blood glucose fluctuations
Avoid repeated multiple injections at the same site to prevent tendon rupture or skin atrophy
NSAIDs require vigilance for the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and are contraindicated in patients with a history of ulcers
personalization: In older adults, topical NSAID gel is preferred to reduce systemic adverse effects
Pregnant women should avoid NSAIDs and corticosteroid injections; splinting and physical therapy are preferred
Patients with occupational hand use need to adjust work posture and prolong immobilization

skills.presentation: Patients complain of persistent dull pain on the lateral aspect of the shoulder, often radiating to the mid-upper arm. A typical finding is the 'painful arc' phenomenon, in which pain worsens during arm abduction from 60° to 120° and lessens after exceeding 120°. Night pain is prominent, and patients have difficulty falling asleep when lying on the affected side. Both active and passive movement are limited, especially external rotation and abduction, with local tender points at the lower border of the acromion and the greater tuberosity of the humerus.

first_questions: Where exactly is your shoulder pain? Does it radiate to the upper arm?
When raising your arm (for example, combing your hair or dressing), at which angle is the pain worst?
Do you wake up at night because of shoulder pain?
followup_questions: Did the pain start suddenly or worsen gradually? Have you recently had activities that overuse the shoulder?
Besides pain, do you feel weakness or catching in the shoulder?
Do you have a history of diabetes, thyroid disease, or rheumatoid arthritis?
stop_conditions: The pain has been clarified as mechanical friction pain without symptoms of nerve injury
The painful arc feature and night pain have been confirmed
History of traumatic fracture and signs of infection have been excluded

essential: Shoulder X-ray (anteroposterior, axillary, and Y views)
Shoulder ultrasound
Physical examination: Neer sign and Hawkins-Kennedy test
if_suspected: Shoulder MRI (when concomitant rotator cuff tear is suspected)
Diagnostic subacromial injection (for differential diagnosis)
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (when septic arthritis is suspected)
avoid: Routine CT scan (low soft-tissue resolution and high radiation; not first-line)
Blind joint aspiration (increases infection risk when there is no evidence of effusion)
Repeated unnecessary radionuclide scans

first_line: First-line treatment includes rest, avoidance of provoking movements, and physical therapy. For pharmacotherapy, NSAIDs are preferred, such as ibuprofen 400mg three times daily or celecoxib 200mg once daily for 7-14 days. Local ice application may be used. If conservative treatment is ineffective, subacromial corticosteroid injection combined with a local anesthetic may be performed, usually no more than 3 times per year. At the same time, rotator cuff strengthening exercises are needed to improve biomechanics.
safety_warnings: Patients with diabetes receiving corticosteroid injections require close monitoring of blood glucose fluctuations
Long-term or high-dose NSAID use requires vigilance for gastrointestinal bleeding and renal impairment
Repeated corticosteroid injections at the same site may cause tendon rupture or fat atrophy
personalization: Use corticosteroid injections with caution in older adults with osteoporosis; physical therapy is preferred
For patients with a history of peptic ulcer, use a COX-2 selective inhibitor together with a proton pump inhibitor
Athletes require a staged rehabilitation plan and should avoid returning to high-intensity exercise too early

skills.presentation: Patients are mostly children, often with a history of falling onto the palm. Typical manifestations are severe elbow pain, marked swelling, and limited movement, with visible local deformity (such as posterior prominence of the elbow or varus/valgus). If accompanied by vascular or nerve injury, ischemic manifestations may occur, such as forearm numbness, pale fingers, decreased skin temperature, or weakened radial artery pulsation.

first_questions: How did you fall when you were injured? Did you land on your palm?
How severe is the elbow pain now? Can you actively move your fingers?
followup_questions: Do your fingers feel numb or have abnormal sensation?
Has the skin color of the hand become pale or purple? Is the temperature lower than on the unaffected side?
stop_conditions: The injury mechanism is clear, and the affected limb has obvious deformity and tenderness
Distal perfusion and neurologic status (such as radial artery pulsation and fingertip sensation) have been confirmed
The patient reports severe pain and is unable to move the joint

essential: Anteroposterior and lateral elbow X-rays
Comparative examination of both upper limbs (inspection and palpation)
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the elbow (to assess comminution and direction of displacement)
Upper-limb vascular ultrasound or CTA (when vascular injury is suspected)
avoid: Repeated forceful passive movement before blind reduction
MRI without indication (X-ray/CT is preferred in the acute phase)

first_line: For nondisplaced or minimally displaced fractures, immobilization with a cast or splint for 4-6 weeks

For marked displacement, closed reduction and percutaneous Kirschner wire fixation under anesthesia are required. After surgery, the affected limb must be strictly elevated to reduce swelling, and perfusion must be closely monitored. Nonpharmacologic interventions include ice application to reduce swelling and early functional exercise of unfixed joints.
safety_warnings: Watch for compartment syndrome; if severe pain and pain on passive stretch occur, immediate fasciotomy and decompression are required
Avoid excessive flexion immobilization, which can compress the median nerve
The exposed Kirschner wire site requires regular dressing changes to prevent infection
personalization: In pediatric patients, protect the growth plate and avoid iatrogenic injury
In older adults with osteoporosis, internal fixation strength may be insufficient; consider augmented fixation methods
Patients with diabetes require strict glycemic control to promote wound healing

skills.presentation: Patients often present with connection of the skin, soft tissue, and even bone between the fingers or toes, resulting in limited movement or abnormal appearance. Typical symptoms include inability to fully separate the affected fingers/toes; some cases are accompanied by nail morphology abnormalities or joint stiffness. Mostly seen in congenital malformations; a small number are caused by scar adhesion after trauma or burns.

first_questions: Did you notice that your child's fingers or toes were joined together at birth?
Is there a family history of similar conditions or other congenital diseases?
followup_questions: If there is functional impairment, which daily activities are specifically affected?
Is there pain, infection, or skin breakdown caused by repeated friction?
stop_conditions: The type and extent of the deformity have been clearly identified, and no further history is needed.
The patient has no functional impairment and no desire for treatment, so in-depth questioning can be stopped.
Necessary physical examination has been completed, and the information is sufficient to formulate an initial plan.

essential: Hand X-ray plain film (to assess bone connection)
Physical examination (observe skin, soft tissue, and joint range of motion)
if_suspected: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (detailed assessment needed for complex bony fusion)
Ultrasound examination (to assist in determining soft tissue layers)
avoid: MRI (not essential unless neurovascular involvement is suspected)
Routine blood tests (unnecessary when there are no signs of infection)

first_line: Surgical treatment is preferred, usually performed at 6-18 months of age. Procedures include Z-plasty, flap transplantation, etc., to separate the syndactyly and restore function. After surgery, the affected limb needs to be immobilized for 4-6 weeks, with rehabilitation training to prevent recurrence of adhesions. Non-pharmacologic interventions include early physical therapy guidance for parents to perform passive movements.
safety_warnings: Avoid surgery that is too early, which may lead to insufficient tissue development.
Be aware of the risk of postoperative infection and maintain strict aseptic technique.
Watch for flap necrosis and closely monitor blood supply.
personalization: For infants and young children, simple procedures are preferred to reduce trauma.
Complex bony fusion requires staged surgery.
For adult patients, psychological needs and expectations for functional improvement need to be assessed.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of foot deformity, presenting as inward turning of the sole (varus), elevated heel unable to touch the ground (equinus), and forefoot adduction. Infants may show asymmetry of both feet or toe-walking and abnormal gait; adults often have pain, callus formation, and difficulty wearing shoes. Typical signs are difficulty passively correcting the foot to a neutral position, high arch, and limited ankle dorsiflexion.

first_questions: Was foot deformity noticed when your child was born?
Is there pain or easy fatigue when walking currently?
Has the patient previously received cast immobilization or surgery?
followup_questions: If there is a family history of similar disease, ask: 'Has any first-degree relative been diagnosed with this condition?'
If accompanied by neurologic symptoms, ask: 'Is there lower limb weakness or decreased sensation?'
If already treated, ask: 'What is the recurrence frequency and current foot range of motion?'
stop_conditions: Congenital deformity has been clearly identified and there is no evidence of nervous system involvement
Imaging examination has confirmed the degree of skeletal structural abnormality
The patient's complaints are highly consistent with physical examination findings and no further differential diagnosis is needed

essential: Weight-bearing X-ray of both feet
Physical examination (Ponseti method to assess stiffness)
Hip and spine examination (to exclude tethered cord, etc.)
if_suspected: Lumbar MRI (suspected neurogenic cause)
Electromyography (assess neuromuscular function)
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction (preoperative planning for complex cases)
avoid: Routine ultrasound (low diagnostic value for bony structures)
Non-weight-bearing X-ray (cannot reflect true load-bearing state)
Unnecessary genetic testing (unless associated with multiple malformations)

first_line: First choice is the Ponseti method: start serial cast correction as early as possible after birth, change casts once weekly, and gradually correct varus and equinus

Most require percutaneous Achilles tenotomy. After surgery, wear an abduction brace (such as Dennis-Browne splint) for 6-9 months, then at night until age 4. Combine with parent-guided foot stretching exercises to prevent recurrence.
safety_warnings: During cast immobilization, closely observe distal blood supply to prevent pressure sores or compartment syndrome
Avoid stopping brace wear too early, which leads to a high recurrence rate
Surgical operation requires precise control of the depth of Achilles tendon release to prevent over-release causing flatfoot
personalization: Intervention in the neonatal period has the best effect; delayed treatment requires a longer casting period
Children with neuromuscular type need combined rehabilitation training and botulinum toxin injection
Older children or adults may require open surgical reconstruction, with individualized plans

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of severe ankle pain, swelling, and inability to bear weight, with bruising rapidly appearing in the foot after injury. Typical manifestations are marked tenderness at the lateral malleolus or behind the medial malleolus, and pain intensifies with passive ankle movement. If accompanied by dislocation, foot deformity and increased skin tension may be seen; some patients may palpate crepitus or abnormal mobility.

first_questions: What was the specific mechanism of injury (e.g., fall from height, crush injury in a car accident)?
Can you still stand or walk after the injury?
Where is the most severe pain located?
followup_questions: Is there numbness or decreased sensation in the foot?
Is there an open wound or blister on the skin at the injured site?
Do you have a history of ankle injury or osteoporosis?
stop_conditions: The injury mechanism has been clearly identified and symptoms are typical, so no further details are needed.
The patient has clearly described the nature of pain and degree of functional limitation.
It has been confirmed that there are no emergency signs of neurovascular compromise.

essential: Anteroposterior and lateral ankle X-rays
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction
Lower extremity vascular ultrasound
if_suspected: MRI examination (assess cartilage injury and blood supply)
Ankle stress X-ray (assess ligament stability)
D-dimer test (screen for deep vein thrombosis risk)
avoid: Blind attempts at manual reduction
Weight-bearing training before fracture is excluded
Unnecessary whole-body radionuclide scanning

first_line: In the acute phase, strict immobilization, elevate the affected limb, and apply ice to reduce swelling. According to fracture type, choose conservative treatment (cast immobilization for 6-12 weeks) or surgical treatment (open reduction and internal fixation). After surgery, long-term weight bearing should be avoided, and X-rays should be repeated regularly to monitor bone healing and signs of femoral head necrosis. During rehabilitation, gradually perform joint range of motion training.
safety_warnings: Be alert for avascular necrosis of the talus; strict avoidance of early weight bearing
Observe dorsalis pedis artery pulsation and skin temperature changes to prevent compartment syndrome
Anticoagulant drugs should be used cautiously, balancing prevention of bleeding and thrombosis
personalization: Elderly patients with osteoporosis need prolonged immobilization and calcium supplementation
Diabetic patients need strict blood glucose control to promote wound healing
Athlete patients need an individualized return-to-sport plan

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of burning, stabbing pain or numbness in the medial sole and heel, with symptoms worsening at night and exacerbated by prolonged walking or standing. Some patients describe discomfort when wearing shoes, which may be slightly relieved by rest or elevating the affected limb. Typical signs include radiating pain induced by tapping the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus (positive Tinel sign).

first_questions: Do you have numbness, tingling, or burning in the sole of your foot or heel?
Are these symptoms more obvious at night when sleeping?
followup_questions: When pressing behind the bone on the inner side of the ankle, do you feel electric shock-like pain radiating to the toes?
Do symptoms worsen after walking for a long time or wearing specific shoes?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes typical medial plantar numbness with nocturnal worsening, and Tinel sign is positive.
It has been confirmed that symptoms are related to weight-bearing activity, and there is no history of systemic neurologic disease.
The patient has provided key history such as previous foot trauma, flatfoot, or diabetes.

essential: Electromyography and nerve conduction velocity studies (assess degree of tibial nerve damage)
High-frequency ultrasound examination (observe nerve swelling and surrounding structures)
Ankle X-ray plain film (exclude bone spur or fracture compression)
if_suspected: Ankle MRI (screen for soft tissue mass, cyst, or inflammation)
Blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin testing (differentiate diabetic peripheral neuropathy)
avoid: Routine lumbar CT (unless accompanied by low back pain or extensive lower limb symptoms)
Unnecessary radionuclide bone scan

first_line: Conservative treatment is preferred: strictly limit strenuous exercise, wear orthopedic insoles to correct flatfoot, and apply local ice. Pharmacologically, oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as celecoxib 200mg/day) or gabapentin (starting at 100mg at bedtime, gradually increasing to 300mg tid) to relieve neuropathic pain. If necessary, perform local block injection (lidocaine combined with corticosteroid), usually for 4-6 weeks. If ineffective, consider surgical release.
safety_warnings: Steroid injection requires strict aseptic technique to avoid damaging the nerve trunk; use cautiously in diabetic patients to prevent blood glucose fluctuations.
Gabapentin may cause dizziness and drowsiness; caution is needed for those driving or working at heights.
Long-term high-dose NSAID use requires attention to the risks of gastrointestinal bleeding and renal impairment.
personalization: Diabetic patients need priority blood glucose control and cautious selection of neurotoxic drugs.
Pregnant women should avoid NSAIDs and steroid injections; physical therapy and brace immobilization are preferred.
Professional athletes need a prolonged conservative treatment period, and postoperative rehabilitation plans need to be individualized.

skills.presentation: Patient reports localized pain at the lateral aspect of the elbow (at the lateral humeral epicondyle), often described as aching or stabbing pain. Pain is markedly aggravated by making a fist, lifting heavy objects, wringing a towel, or extending the wrist, and may be relieved by rest. Some patients have weakness of the forearm extensor muscles, and in severe cases daily grasping actions are affected, with marked tenderness on local palpation.

first_questions: When exactly did the pain on the lateral side of your elbow start?
Have you recently performed frequent arm activities, such as playing ball, lifting heavy objects, or repetitive labor?
followup_questions: Is the pain worsened when you forcefully bend your wrist upward or hold a cup?
Do you also feel pain at night while resting, or does it affect your sleep?
stop_conditions: The pain has been clearly localized to the lateral elbow and is associated with specific movements.
It has been confirmed that there is no history of trauma and no symptoms of radiating nerve pain.
The previous treatment course and the current degree of functional limitation have been ascertained.

essential: Physical examination of the elbow (Cozen test, Mill test)
Plain radiography of the elbow (to exclude bony lesions)
if_suspected: Musculoskeletal ultrasound (to assess the degree of tendon degeneration and tearing)
MRI (when concomitant ligament injury or complex lesions are suspected)
avoid: Routine CT scanning (low soft-tissue resolution and high radiation exposure)
Unnecessary systemic blood inflammatory marker screening (when there are no signs of infection)

first_line: First-line conservative treatment: strict immobilization during the acute phase and wearing an elbow brace, together with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., ibuprofen 0.2g tid or celecoxib 0.2qd) for 7-14 days

Local physical therapy may be given (ultrasound, shockwave). During the chronic phase, eccentric strength training should be performed. Avoid excessive loading activities; the treatment course usually requires 4-6 weeks to show effect.
safety_warnings: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with peptic ulcer disease or renal insufficiency.
Watch for gastrointestinal adverse reactions to the medication; taking it after meals is recommended.
Avoid long-term continuous local corticosteroid injections to prevent tendon rupture.
personalization: Use NSAIDs with caution in older adults; topical preparations are preferred.
Patients with diabetes need blood glucose monitoring and cautious use of corticosteroid injections.
Professional athletes require a staged rehabilitation plan for return to sport.

skills.presentation: Patients often have a clear history of trauma or surgery, with progressive local swelling, pain, and restricted joint movement occurring weeks to months after injury. The typical presentation is a hard mass palpable within the muscle that gradually calcifies over time, leading to stiffness of the adjacent joint. Early symptoms are easily confused with a hematoma, but later the mass becomes firmer with indistinct borders, and X-ray shows irregular high-density shadows within the soft tissues.

first_questions: What were the exact time and site of the injury or surgery?
Have you recently felt persistently worsening pain or swelling at the affected site?
Has your joint range of motion decreased significantly compared with before the injury?
followup_questions: If the mass becomes more painful at night, is it accompanied by fever?
Do you have any previous similar history or family predisposition?
Did you undergo vigorous rehabilitation training too early after the injury?
stop_conditions: There is a clear history of trauma together with typical progressive joint stiffness and a mass.
Imaging has shown characteristic ossification.
Infectious complications have been excluded (e.g., high fever, markedly elevated white blood cell count).

essential: Plain radiography of the affected limb (anteroposterior and lateral views)
Ultrasound examination (to assess soft-tissue vascularity and cystic versus solid nature)
CT scanning (three-dimensional reconstruction to assess the degree of ossification)
if_suspected: MRI (to differentiate tumor or deep hematoma)
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (to exclude infection)
Bone scan (to assess metabolic activity)
avoid: Blind open biopsy in the early phase (may induce and aggravate ossification)
Overreliance on repeated high-dose irradiation before radionuclide therapy
Forceful passive stretching before a definite diagnosis

first_line: During the acute phase, strict immobilization and cold compresses are required, and massage and vigorous active/passive exercise should be avoided. After the ossification matures (usually 6-12 months), if it severely affects function, surgical excision of the heterotopic bone tissue is performed. Before surgery, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., indomethacin) may be considered to prevent recurrence, for a course of about 4-6 weeks. After surgery, gentle functional exercise should be combined to prevent adhesions.
safety_warnings: Surgical excision is strictly prohibited before the ossification has matured; otherwise recurrence is highly likely.
With NSAIDs, be alert to the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, especially in older patients.
Avoid deep massage or forceful physical therapy at the affected site to prevent stimulation of bone formation.
personalization: In pediatric patients, attention should be paid to effects on growth and development, and the timing of surgery should be chosen more cautiously.
Patients with spinal cord injury have sensory impairment and require intensified skin care to prevent pressure ulcers.
Patients with coagulation disorders require adjustment of the anticoagulation regimen before surgical intervention.

skills.presentation: Patients often report dull pain in a single joint (e.g., knee, hip) that is chronic and progressively worsening, accompanied by low-grade fever, night sweats, and fatigue. There is local swelling but skin temperature is not elevated, without acute redness, swelling, heat, or pain. In advanced stages, joint deformity, restricted movement, or sinus tract formation may occur, with thin pus containing caseous material. Symptoms are insidious and easily misdiagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis or septic arthritis.

first_questions: How long has the joint pain lasted? Have you had night sweats or unexplained low-grade fever?
Do you have a recent history of pulmonary tuberculosis or close contact with a case?
Has the joint become swollen, stiff, or restricted in movement?
followup_questions: If there is joint drainage or a sinus tract, ask about the character of the discharge and its duration.
If there are systemic symptoms, ask further about weight loss and previous antituberculosis treatment history.
If spinal involvement is suspected, ask whether there is lower-limb numbness or bowel/bladder dysfunction.
stop_conditions: There is a clear history of tuberculosis contact and typical joint symptoms have persisted for more than 3 months.
Imaging shows bone destruction with features of a cold abscess, and ESR/CRP are markedly elevated.
The patient has received standard antituberculosis treatment and has shown a therapeutic response.

essential: Plain joint radiography (to observe bone erosion and joint space narrowing)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) testing
Smear of joint aspirate for acid-fast bacilli and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
if_suspected: MRI (to assess the extent of soft-tissue abscess and bone marrow edema)
PPD skin test or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA)
Chest CT (to screen for primary pulmonary lesions)
avoid: Unnecessary intra-articular corticosteroid injection (may spread infection)
Blind incision and drainage before etiological confirmation
Empirical use of broad-spectrum antibiotics without bacterial culture

first_line: First-line standard four-drug antituberculosis chemotherapy: isoniazid (300mg/d), rifampicin (450-600mg/d), pyrazinamide (750-1000mg/d), and ethambutol (750-1000mg/d), with a 2-month intensive phase and a consolidation phase of at least 10 months. In the early stage, bed rest and immobilization are required, with plaster fixation if necessary
In advanced cases with severe joint destruction, debridement of the lesion or joint fusion is required.
safety_warnings: It is strictly prohibited to use glucocorticoids alone without antituberculosis treatment.
Be aware of interactions between rifampicin and many drugs (e.g., warfarin, oral contraceptives).
Monitor liver function regularly, and watch for isoniazid-induced peripheral neuritis and hepatotoxicity.
personalization: In pediatric patients, doses must be calculated precisely by body weight to avoid ethambutol-induced optic nerve damage.
In older adults or patients with renal insufficiency, the doses of pyrazinamide and aminoglycosides need adjustment.
Streptomycin is contraindicated in pregnant women; a regimen of isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol may be selected.

skills.presentation: Patients often report numbness and tingling in the little finger and the ulnar side of the ring finger, as well as hand weakness. The typical presentation is claw hand deformity, namely hyperextension of the 4th and 5th metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints. Fine motor impairment is prominent, such as inability to button clothing or pinch a piece of paper. Symptoms worsen after a history of elbow or wrist trauma, and numbness is pronounced at night.

first_questions: Do your little finger and ring finger have persistent numbness or an electric shock-like sensation?
Do you feel weakness in your hand, and can you easily pinch a piece of paper or button clothing?
Before the symptoms appeared, did you have any elbow or wrist trauma or a history of prolonged pressure?
followup_questions: Is the numbness worse at night or when you bend your elbow?
Has there been muscle wasting in the hand, especially in the web space between the thumb and index finger or the hypothenar region?
Does the pain radiate to the medial aspect of the forearm?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described typical ulnar sensory impairment and intrinsic hand muscle weakness.
A clear history of cubital tunnel or wrist compression/trauma has been confirmed.
The duration of symptoms and aggravating factors have been fully documented.

essential: Tinel sign test (percussion over the cubital tunnel at the elbow or Guyon canal at the wrist)
Froment sign test (to assess adductor pollicis function)
Electrophysiological testing of intrinsic hand muscle strength and sensory distribution (nerve conduction velocity)
if_suspected: Elbow X-ray (to exclude bone spurs, fracture, or cubitus valgus deformity)
High-resolution ultrasound or MRI (to assess the site of nerve compression and soft-tissue lesions)
Electromyography (EMG) to localize the level of injury and assess severity
avoid: Routine lumbar CT/MRI (not first-line unless accompanied by low back and leg pain)
Nontargeted systemic vitamin B12 level screening (unless there is a clear history of nutritional deficiency)
Repeated nonspecific blood inflammatory marker testing

first_line: For mild cases, conservative treatment is preferred: avoid prolonged elbow flexion, wear an extension-position brace at night, and take oral mecobalamin (0.5mg three times daily) and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., celecoxib 200mg once daily) to relieve symptoms. For moderate-to-severe cases or progressive muscle atrophy, surgical decompression or neurolysis is required, followed by rehabilitation training to restore hand function.
safety_warnings: Long-term use of NSAIDs requires attention to the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding; taking them after meals is recommended.
Mecobalamin is contraindicated in patients allergic to it, and the dose must be adjusted in patients with renal insufficiency.
With surgical decompression, be alert to iatrogenic nerve injury and postoperative scar adhesions.
personalization: Patients with diabetes need strict blood glucose control to promote nerve repair.
In older patients, pay attention to osteoporosis risk and avoid excessive immobilization leading to joint stiffness.
Those with occupational repetitive strain need to adjust their work posture or change jobs.
